Categorical action for finite classical groups and its applications: characteristic 0
Pengcheng Li, Peng Shan and Jiping Zhang

Abstract
. In this paper, we construct a categorical double quantum Heisenberg action on the representation category of finite classical groups O 2 ​ n + 1 ⁡ ( q ) \operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q) , Sp 2 ​ n ⁡ ( q ) \operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q) and O 2 ​ n ± ⁡ ( q ) \operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q) with q q odd. Over a field of characteristic zero or characteristic ℓ \ell with ℓ ∤ q ⁡ ( q − 1 ) \ell\nmid q(q-1) , we deduce a categorical action of a Kac-Moody algebra 𝔰 ​ 𝔩 I + ′ ⊕ 𝔰 ​ 𝔩 I − ′ \mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}} on the representation category of finite classical groups. We show that the colored weight functions 𝕆 + ​ ( u ) ​ ( − ) \mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-) , 𝕆 − ​ ( v ) ​ ( − ) \mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-) and uniform projection can distinguish all irreducible characters of finite classical groups. In particular, the colored weight functions are complete invariants of quadratic unipotent characters. We also show that using the theta correspondence and extra symmetries of categorical double quantum Heisenberg action, the Kac-Moody action on the Grothendieck group of the whole category can be determined explicitly.



2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
20C15, 20C33

Introduction

0.1.
Overview

Let
\mathbf{G}
be a connected reductive algebraic group defined over a finite field
\mathbb{F}_{q}
. The finite
group
G=\mathbf{G}(\mathbb{F}_{q})
of its
\mathbb{F}_{q}
-rational points is a finite reductive group.
When the center of
\mathbf{G}
is connected, Lusztig in his book
[
45
]

classified all irreducible characters of finite reductive groups by using
Deligne–Lusztig theory, Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials,
perverse sheaves, cell theory for Hecke algebras, etc. Lusztig
[
46
]
extended this
to the disconnected center case via the so-called regular embedding from
G
to a larger group

\widetilde{G}
with connected center. The classification is given in terms of
restriction from irreducible characters of
\widetilde{G}
to
G
, which is multiplicity-free. However,
there is no natural way to distinguish all the components of this restriction.
So the classification of irreducible characters of the finite reductive group with disconnected center is not complete in some sense. In this paper,
we focus on the representation theory of finite classical groups
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q),

\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q).
The connected components of the latter two groups have disconnected center. One of the aims of this article is to give a complete classification of the irreducible characters of those groups by using categorification methods.

Categorification has played a prominent role in the recent development of representation theory.
The pioneering work of Chuang–Rouquier
[
14
]
introduced the notion of an
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{2}
-categorification (a.k.a. a categorical
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{2}
-action), and solved Broué’s abelian defect group conjecture
[
5
]
for symmetric groups
S_{n}
and finite general linear groups
\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{n}(q)
using this new tool. Later, Khovanov and Lauda
[
38
]
and Rouquier
[
55
]
independently extended this notion to arbitrary symmetrizable Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{g}
by introducing a remarkable new
2
-category
\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{g})
in terms of generators and relations. Their
2
-categories were originally defined in different forms, it was shown by Brundan
[
6
]
that they are actually equivalent. However, it is difficult to construct direct actions of these
2
-categories on representation categories, as the invertibility of certain
2
-morphisms is impossible to check in general. But, when
\mathfrak{g}
is of type
A
or affine type
A
, Rouquier (based on previous work of Chuang–Rouquier
[
14
]
) showed that one can avoid such difficulties using a control from the Grothendieck group
[
55
, Theorem 5.23]
.
In particular, the construction of
[
14
]
really yields a categorical action of
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I}
on the unipotent blocks of
\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{n}(q)
.

For the finite classical groups
\operatorname{GU}\nolimits_{n}(q),

\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
and
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q),

Dudas, Varagnolo and Vasserot
[
20
,
19
]
constructed an
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I}
-categorification on unipotent blocks using a similar approach and proved that
Broué’s conjecture is true
for the unipotent blocks of these groups at linear primes.
Inspired by the reduction theorem of Bonnafé-Dat-Rouquier
[
3
, Theorem 7.7]
,
Liu and two of the authors
[
39
]
constructed a categorical action of a Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I^{\prime}}
on isolated blocks of
\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
which generalizes the previous works
[
14
,
20
,
19
]
and confirmed
Broué’s conjecture for all the blocks of
\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
at linear primes.

However, all these works rely on
the result of Fong-Srinivasan
[
21
,
22
]
about
the block theory of classical groups with connected center. Due to the nonconnectedness of the center, the block distribution of characters of
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{\pm}(q)
is not completely determined. This is an essential difficulty to generalize the above construction to these groups, since one needs to know the coincidence of the weight space decomposition and the block decomposition in order to get the desired categorical action from Rouquier’s approach.

We overcome the above difficulty using a new method of categorical type
A
or affine type
A
Kac-Moody algebras via Heisenberg categories. This method is due to Brundan, Savage and Webster
[
10
]
. The Heisenberg category
\mathcal{H}eis_{m}(z)
of central charge
m\in\mathbb{Z}
is a monoidal category constructed from degenerate affine Hecke algebras or affine Hecke algebras and it comes in two forms, degenerate or quantum, depending on the parameter
z
. It is called degenerate if
z=0
and quantum if
z\neq 0
. They are introduced respectively by Brundan
[
7
]
and Brundan, Savage and Webster
[
9
]
, generalizing previous works of Khovanov
[
37
]
in the degenerate case
m=-1
, Licata and Savage
[
41
]
in the quantum case
m=-1
and Mackaay and Savage
[
47
]
in the degenerate case
m<0
.

In our situation, to construct the desired Kac-Moody action on representations of
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q),

\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{\pm}(q)
, we consider
a “double version” of the quantum Heisenberg category, which is a symmetric product of two quantum Heisenberg categories. We prove that this category acts on the category of representations of these groups, and using similar ideas as in
[
10
]
, we deduce a categorical action of Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I^{\prime}}
, which is a “double version” of a
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I}
-categorification and has been observed in the previous work
[
39
]
by Liu and two of the authors. Note that our construction is valid over any coefficient ring
R
for representations of
G
. Moreover, it applies also to all the previous situations as well, and provides a uniform way to construct categorical
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I^{\prime}}
-actions on the whole category of representations of finite classical groups
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q),

\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
.

Furthermore, the categorical double quantum Heisenberg action gives rise to some new invariants
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-)
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-)
on the representation category. In this paper, we use them together with the uniform projection to give a complete classification of irreducible modules of
finite classical groups
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
in characteristic zero, hence completing the classification of Lusztig.

Now, let us discuss the main content of the paper.

0.2.
Categorical actions

Throughout this paper,
we always assume that
\ell
is a prime,
K
is a field of characteristic 0,
\mathcal{O}
is a complete discrete valuation ring and
k
is a field of characteristic
\ell
. Let
R=K,

\mathcal{O}
or
k
such that
q(q-1)
is invertible in
R
and
q^{1/2},\sqrt{-1}\in R
.
Let
V
be a finite-dimensional symplectic or orthogonal space over the field
\mathbb{F}_{q}
of
odd characteristic
p
.
Let
G_{n}
be one of the families of finite classical groups among
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q),\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
,
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{+}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{-}(q)
such that
G_{n}
is an isometry group of symplectic or orthogonal space
V
.
Using the tower of natural inclusions of groups

\cdots\subset G_{n-1}\subset G_{n}\subset G_{n+1}\subset\cdots,

one can form the abelian categories

RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits:=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}RG_{n}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits

of representations
of all the groups
G_{n}
with
n
running over

\mathbb{N}^{*}=\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
in the

\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{-}(q)
case and
\mathbb{N}^{*}=\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
in all the other cases.
Based on the construction of the representation datum by Liu and two of the authors in
[
39
]
, we proved the following theorem.

Theorem A
.

Let
R
be one of
K
,
\mathcal{O}
and
k
, then there is a strict
R
-linear monoidal functor

\Psi:\,\mathcal{H}eis_{-2}(z^{+},t^{+})\odot\mathcal{H}eis_{-2}(z^{-},t^{-})\to\mathcal{E}nd(RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits).

Here
\mathcal{H}eis_{-2}(z^{+},t^{+})\odot\mathcal{H}eis_{-2}(z^{-},t^{-})
is a symmetric product of two quantum Heisenberg categories
\mathcal{H}eis_{-2}(z^{+},t^{+})
and
\mathcal{H}eis_{-2}(z^{-},t^{-})
, which is called
double quantum Heisenberg category
in this article (see §
1.5
), and

\mathcal{E}nd(RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits)
is the strict monoidal category consisting of
endofunctors and natural transformations of
RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
. The parameters
z^{\pm}
and
t^{\pm}
are defined at the beginning of §
2
.

In
[
32
]
, Huang, Shen and the first author proved that the categorical action of a
symmetric product

\mathcal{H}eis_{-2}(z^{+},t^{+})\odot\mathcal{H}eis_{-2}(z^{-},t^{-})
over a field
can be strengthened to a categorical action of a Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{g}
with disjoint union quivers
of type
A
by generalizing the corresponding results in
[
10
,
39
]
, where
\mathfrak{g}
is uniquely determined by this categorical action (see §
1.5
).
Using Lusztig’s Jordan decomposition and Howlett–Lehrer theory, we can determine the associated Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
for the categorical double quantum Heisenberg action in Theorem A, which is a direct sum of two Kac-Moody algebras of type
A
, where

I_{+}=q^{\mathbb{Z}}\sqcup-q^{\mathbb{Z}}~~\text{and}~~I_{-}=q^{\mathbb{Z}}\sqcup-q^{\mathbb{Z}}

as subsets of
R
(see Proposition
4.9
).
The construction in
[
32
]
endows
RG\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
with a structure of
\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{g})
-categorification, so we have the following corollary.

Corollary B
.

Let
R=K
or
k
, then there is a strict
R
-linear monoidal functor

\Psi^{\prime}:\,\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}})\to\mathcal{E}nd(RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits).

In fact, the above construction also applies to
\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{n}(q)
and
\operatorname{GU}\nolimits_{n}(q)
by a similar argument.
In particular, for
R=k
, we get this categorical action without using the basic set properties for unipotent or quadratic unipotent modules of finite reductive groups
[
21
,
24
,
25
]
and the classification of blocks of finite classical groups by Fong and Srinivasan
[
21
,
22
]
.

The Kac-Moody categorification is also helpful for other problems in modular representation theory of finite classical groups, for example, modular Harish-Chandra theory (see
[
20
,
49
]
) and calculating the decomposition numbers (see
[
17
,
18
]
).

0.3.
Applications to classifications of irreducible modules in characteristic zero

One of the advantages of double quantum Heisenberg category is that there are two central
elements
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)\in{\operatorname{End}}(\mathds{1})((u^{-1}))
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)\in{\operatorname{End}}(\mathds{1})((v^{-1}))
, where
\mathds{1}
is the identity functor, and
u
and
v
are two indeterminates (see §
1.3
). Let
R=K
or
k
be an algebraically closed field. For each irreducible module

L\in RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
, we consider the action of
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)
on
\mathds{1}(L)=L
. By Schur’s lemma,
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(L)\in R((u^{-1}))
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(L)\in R((v^{-1})).
So we get the following functions, and we call them
colored weight functions

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-):\,{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits)\to R((u^{-1})),\quad\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-):\,{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits)\to R((v^{-1})).

They contain all the information on the weight space decomposition of the Kac-Moody
categorification.

From now on, let
R=K
be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0. Let
{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G)
denote the set of irreducible modules of
KG
, or equivalently, the irreducible characters of
G.
Let
\mathcal{V}(G)
be the space of class function on
G
,
and let
\mathcal{V}(G)^{\sharp}
denote the subspace spanned by Deligne-Lusztig virtual characters (see §
4.1.2
).
For
f\in\mathcal{V}(G)
the orthogonal projection of
f
onto
\mathcal{V}(G)^{\sharp}

is denoted by
f^{\sharp}
and called the
uniform projection
.
A class function
f\in\mathcal{V}(G)
is called
uniform
if
f^{\sharp}=f
. In fact, for
\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{n}(q)
and
\operatorname{GU}\nolimits_{n}(q)
, since all irreducible characters are uniform, we can distinguish irreducible modules of these two groups by using the uniform projection. However, this is not true for
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q),

\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q),
see
[
53
]
for a detailed discussion.
Using extra symmetries constructed in §
3
,
we can show that colored weight functions together with the uniform projection can distinguish all
irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal (see §
4.2
) and
then all irreducible modules (see §
4.3.5
).
In fact, we have the following theorem.

Theorem C
.

Let
G_{n}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
,
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
or
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{\pm}(q)
and
\rho,\rho^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G_{n}).

(a)

We have
\rho=\rho^{\prime}
if and only if the following hold:

(1)

\rho^{\sharp}=\rho^{\prime\sharp},

(2)

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\prime})
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{\prime}).

(b)

If
\rho
and
\rho^{\prime}
are quadratic unipotent, then
\rho=\rho^{\prime}
if and only if

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\prime})
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{\prime}).

(c)

If
\rho
and
\rho^{\prime}
are unipotent, then
\rho=\rho^{\prime}
if and only if

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\prime}).

Theorem C implies that using uniform projection and the
colored weight functions
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-)
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-)
,
we can give a complete characterisation for irreducible modules of finite classical groups
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q),

\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
in characteristic zero. Moreover, the colored weight functions
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-)
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-)
are complete invariants of quadratic unipotent modules
and the colored weight function
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-)

is a complete invariant of unipotent modules.

In order to prove Theorem C, we try to compare the Grothendieck group of
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
with a direct sum of tensor products of Fock space representations of the Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}.
Since the action is integrable, it is enough to determine the highest weight vectors which are given by the classes of irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal. Using the categorical Kac-Moody action and the extra symmetries, we can determine these highest weights up to some signatures. See Theorem
4.21
for more details.

0.4.
Theta correspondence

In the last part of the paper, we study an interesting connection between theta correspondence and the categorical Kac-Moody actions on finite classical groups.

Let us introduce the theta correspondence over finite fields now.
Let
(G,G^{\prime})
be a reductive dual pair over a finite field
\mathbb{F}_{q}
of odd characteristic.
Restricting the Weil character (
[
28
]
) to
(G,G^{\prime})
with respect to
a nontrivial additive character
\psi
of
\mathbb{F}_{q}
,
we have the
Weil character

\omega^{\psi}_{G,G^{\prime}}
,
which has the non-negative integral decomposition

\omega^{\psi}_{G,G^{\prime}}=\sum_{\rho\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G),\rho^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G^{\prime})}m_{\rho,\rho^{\prime}}\rho\otimes\rho^{\prime}.

We say that
(\rho,\rho^{\prime})

occurs
in the
theta correspondence
(or
Howe correspondence
) if
m_{\rho,\rho^{\prime}}\neq 0
,
i.e., there is a relation

\displaystyle\Theta^{\psi}_{G,G^{\prime}}=\{\,(\rho,\rho^{\prime})\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G)\times{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G^{\prime})\mid m_{\rho,\rho^{\prime}}\neq 0\,\}

between
{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G)
and
{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G^{\prime})
.
The finite theta correspondence has been studied in
[
31
,
56
,
1
,
2
,
50
,
51
,
52
,
53
,
54
,
42
,
48
]
.

We use the theta correspondence to remove the ambiguity of signatures in Theorem
4.21
, hence we obtain a complete description of the action of Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
on the Grothendieck group of
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
(see §
5
).
The main idea is the following.
First, we note that theta cuspidal (as defined in
[
48
, §1.8]
) is equivalent to being
F^{+}
-cuspidal or
F^{-}
-cuspidal;
see Lemma
5.6
. Then
extra symmetries constructed in §
3
reduce this problem to theta cuspidal modules.
By the work of Pan
[
52
]
, together with Adams and Moy
[
1
]
, the theta correspondence for the first occurrence of theta cuspidal modules can be determined up to a twist of the sign character.
Finally, the signatures in colored weight functions of theta cuspidal modules can be obtained using a formula from the work of Ma, Qiu and Zou
[
48
]
.

This provides a new approach, which is of characteristic 0, to determine the Kac-Moody action on the Grothendieck group of representation of finite classical groups, see Theorem
5.13
and Theorem
5.16
.
Note that all the previous works, such as

[
20
,
19
,
39
]
for unipotent or quadratic unipotent modules, use a different approach which relies on the Brauer tree theory of finite classical groups
[
23
]
in positive characteristic.

It’s worth mentioning that the categorical Kac-Moody action and the theta correspondence for finite classical groups are deeply connected. In fact, by
[
19
]
, the
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}
-action on the Grothendieck group of unipotent modules of finite symplectic groups was known, then one can recover the symplectic-even orthogonal theta correspondence for unipotent modules by
[
48
, Theorem 1.3]
, see Remark
5.11
.

0.5.
Future work

In our next paper
[
40
]
, we will use the tools developed here to study modular representations of
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
. More precisely, using the reduction modulo
\ell
of colored weight functions
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-)
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-)
, we will complete the determination of the
\ell
-block distribution of characters of
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
. Furthermore, based on the Kac-Moody categorification in Theorem B, we will prove that Broué’s conjecture is also true
for the remaining finite classical groups
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
at linear primes.

0.6.
Organization of the paper

The paper is organized as follows.
In Section
1
, we collect basic concepts and notations, which
include quantum Heisenberg category,
the symmetric product of monoidal categories, double
quantum Heisenberg category, etc.
In Section
2
, we construct a categorical double
quantum Heisenberg action on
\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}RG_{n}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits

for groups
G_{n}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
,
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{\pm}(q)
with
R\in(K,\mathcal{O},k)
which is Theorem A
and a categorical Kac-Moody action on
\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}RG_{n}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits

with
R=K
or
k
.
In Section
3
, we study the
extra symmetries of the above categorical double
quantum Heisenberg action and categorical Kac-Moody action.
In Section
4
, we recall some basic facts on the classifications of irreducible characters of finite classical groups by Lusztig and prove Theorem B. We also show that colored weight functions
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-)
,
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-)

and uniform projection can distinguish all irreducible modules, and prove Theorem C.
In Section
5
, we introduce the theta correspondence and
then we show that using theta correspondence we can determine the Kac-Moody action on the Grothendieck group
[KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]
.

While we were writing this paper, Sergio David Cía Luvecce informed us that he
also constructed a Kac-Moody categorification for the unipotent blocks of
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)

by a different method.

1.
Preliminaries

In this section, we collect some preliminaries about
quantum Heisenberg categories, symmetric product of monoidal categories and double quantum Heisenberg categories.

1.1.
Algebras and categories

An
R
-category

\mathscr{C}
is an additive category enriched over the tensor
category of
R
-modules. As usual, we write
EF
or
E\circ F
for a composition of functors
E
and
F
,
and
\psi\circ\phi
for a composition of
morphisms of functors (or natural transformations)
\psi
and
\phi
.
Also, we denote by
\mathds{1}=\mathds{1}_{\mathscr{C}}
the identity functor on
\mathscr{C}
,
and by
1_{F}
or
\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{F}
the identity element in the endomorphism
ring
{\operatorname{End}}(F)
.

Let
\mathscr{C}
be an abelian
R
-category.
We denote by
[\mathscr{C}]
the complexified Grothendieck group of
\mathscr{C}
,
by
[M]
the class of an object
M
of
\mathscr{C}
in
[\mathscr{C}]
,
and by
[F]
the linear map on
[\mathscr{C}]
induced by an exact endofunctor
F
of
\mathscr{C}
.

If the Hom spaces of
\mathscr{C}
are finitely generated over
R
, then
the category
\mathscr{C}
is called Hom-finite. In this case, we set
\mathscr{H}(M)={\operatorname{End}}_{\mathscr{C}}(M)^{\text{op}}
for an object
M\in\mathscr{C}
,
so that
\mathscr{H}(M)
is an
R
-algebra which is finitely generated as an
R
-module.
An
R
-category
\mathscr{C}
is a

locally finite abelian category
if

\mathscr{C}
is abelian, all objects are of finite length, and Hom-finite.

Now let
A
be an
R
-algebra that is free and finitely generated over
R
.
Let
\mathscr{C}=A\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
. We write
{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(\mathscr{C})
or
{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(A)
for
the set of isomorphism classes of simple objects of

.

We will use the string calculus for strict monoidal categories
and strict 2-categories
as explained in
[
57
, Chapter 2]
.
Let
\mathscr{A}
be a strict
R
-linear monoidal category. A (strict)
module category over
\mathscr{A}

is a
R
-linear category
\mathscr{C}
together with a strict
R
-linear monoidal functor

\Phi:\mathscr{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}nd(\mathscr{C})
, where

\mathcal{E}nd(\mathscr{C})
denotes the strict
R
-linear monoidal
category with objects that are
R
-linear endofunctors of
\mathscr{C}
and morphisms
that are natural transformations.
We usually suppress the monoidal functor
\Phi
, using the same notation

f:E\rightarrow F
both for
a morphism in
\mathscr{A}
and for
the natural transformation
between endofunctors of
\mathscr{C}
that is its image under
\Phi
.
The evaluation
f_{V}:EV\rightarrow FV

of this natural transformation
on an object
V\in\mathscr{C}
will be represented diagrammatically by drawing a
line labeled by

V
on the right-hand side of the usual string diagram

1.3.
From Heisenberg categorification to Kac-Moody categorification

In this section, we will recall some notations and results in
[
10
]
.

Definition 1.2
.

A
categorical quantum Heisenberg action
on a locally finite category
\mathcal{C}
is the data
of a strict monoidal functor
\mathcal{H}eis_{k}(z,t)\rightarrow\mathcal{E}nd(\mathcal{C})
, where

\mathcal{E}nd(\mathcal{C})
is the strict monoidal category consisting of
endofunctors and natural transformations.

In this section, we assume that
R
is a field.
Now we assume that there exists a categorical quantum Heisenberg action
on a locally finite category
\mathcal{C}.

Let
L\in\mathcal{C}
be an irreducible object. We can define
m_{L}(u),n_{L}(u)\in R[u]
to
be the (monic)
minimal polynomials
of
the endomorphisms

By adjunction, it follows that

The discussion above shows that

(1.11)

\displaystyle E

\displaystyle F

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{i\in I}F_{i},

and

are non-zero.

For an irreducible object
L\in\mathcal{C}
,
it was showed in
[
10
, Lemma 4.17]
that

\mathbb{O}(u)(L)=m_{L}(u)/n_{L}(u).

Moreover, the constant terms of
the polynomials
m_{L}(u)
and
n_{L}(u)
satisfy
t^{2}=m_{L}(0)/n_{L}(0)
.

It was shown in
[
10
, Lemma 4.6]
,

i\in I
if and only if
qi\in I
.
Let
1\neq q\in R^{\times}
and
{I}
be a (possibly infinite) subset of
R^{\times}
.
To the pair
({I},q)
we associate a (not necessarily connected)
quiver
{I}(q)
(also denoted by
{I}
) as follows:

•

the vertex set is
{I}
, and

•

there is an arrow
i\to i\cdot q

if and only if
i,i\cdot q\in{I}
.

Now assume that
{I}
is stable under the multiplication by
q
and
q^{-1}
.
If
q
is a primitive
e
-th root of unity
then the quiver
{I}(q)
is the disjoint union of cyclic quivers of type
A_{e-1}^{(1)}
,
while if
q
is not a root of unity then
{I}(q)

is the disjoint union of quivers of type
A_{\infty}
.

The quiver
{I}(q)
defines a symmetric generalized Cartan matrix

A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in{I}}
with

\begin{cases}a_{ii}=2&\\
a_{ij}=-1&\text{if}~i\rightarrow j~\text{or}~j\rightarrow i\\
a_{ij}=0&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

To this Cartan matrix one can
associate the Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{{I}}^{\prime}
over
\mathbb{C}
, which
has Chevalley generators
e_{i},f_{i}
for
i\in{I}
, subject to the usual
relations.
For
i\in{I}
, let
\alpha_{i},

\alpha^{\vee}_{i}
be the simple root and coroot
corresponding to
e_{i}
and let
\Lambda_{i}
be the
i
-th fundamental weight. Recall that

\operatorname{X}\nolimits^{\vee}=\bigoplus\limits_{i\in{I}}\mathbb{Z}\alpha_{i}^{\vee}
and

\operatorname{X}\nolimits=\bigoplus\limits_{i\in{I}}\mathbb{Z}\Lambda_{i}.

For an irreducible object
L\in\mathcal{C}
, let

(1.16)

{\operatorname{wt}}(L):=\sum_{i\in I}(\phi_{i}(L)-\epsilon_{i}(L))\Lambda_{i}\in\operatorname{X}\nolimits.

Then for
\lambda\in\operatorname{X}\nolimits
we let
\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}
be the Serre
subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
consisting of the objects
V

such that every irreducible subquotient
L
of
V

satisfies
{\operatorname{wt}}(L)=\lambda
.
The point of this definition is
that irreducible objects
K,L\in\mathcal{C}
with
{\operatorname{wt}}(K)\neq{\operatorname{wt}}(L)

have different central characters.
Using also the general theory of blocks,
it follows that

(1.17)

\textstyle\mathcal{C}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in X}\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}.

We call it the
weight space

decomposition of
\mathcal{C}
.

Theorem 1.3

(
[
10
]
)
.

Let
R=K
or
k.

Associated with
\mathcal{C}
,
there is a
2
-representation

\Phi:\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I})\rightarrow\mathfrak{Cat}_{R}

defined on objects by

\lambda\mapsto\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}
,
on generating
1-morphisms by

E_{i}1_{\lambda}\mapsto E_{i}|_{\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}}

and
F_{i}1_{\lambda}\mapsto F_{i}|_{\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}}
for
i\in I.

We refer readers to
[
10
, Theorem 4.11]
for a more detailed and explicit explanation.

1.4.
Double quantum Heisenberg category

In this section, we will consider the symmetric product of two quantum Heisenberg categories.

Now let us introduce the concept of the symmetric product of two monoidal categories (see for example
[
11
]
).
Given a strict
R
-linear monoidal categories
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
, we can form their free product
\mathcal{C}\circledast\mathcal{D}
as a strict
R
-linear monoidal category. This can be defined by the following universal property: the category of
R
-linear monoidal functors
\mathcal{C}\circledast\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{B}
for any other strict
R
-linear monoidal category
\mathcal{B}
is the same as the category of pairs of
R
-linear monoidal functors
\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{B}
. When
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
are themselves defined by generators and relations, the free product of
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
may be constructed simply as the strict
R
-linear monoidal category defined by taking the disjoint union of the given generators and relations of
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
.
The
symmetric product

\mathcal{C}\odot\mathcal{D}
is the strict
R
-linear monoidal
category obtained from
\mathcal{C}\circledast\mathcal{D}
by
adjoining isomorphisms
\sigma_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}Y\otimes X

such that
\sigma_{Y,X}=\sigma_{X,Y}^{-1}

for each pair of objects
X\in\mathcal{C}
and
Y\in\mathcal{D}
,
subject also to the relations

\displaystyle\sigma_{X_{1}\otimes X_{2},Y}

\displaystyle=(\sigma_{X_{1},Y}\otimes 1_{X_{2}})\circ(1_{X_{1}}\otimes\sigma_{X_{2},Y}),

\displaystyle\sigma_{X_{2},Y}\circ(f\otimes 1_{Y})

\displaystyle=(1_{Y}\otimes f)\circ\sigma_{X_{1},Y},

\displaystyle\sigma_{X,Y_{1}\otimes Y_{2}}

\displaystyle=(1_{Y_{1}}\otimes\sigma_{X,Y_{2}})\circ(\sigma_{X,Y_{1}}\otimes 1_{Y_{2}}),

\displaystyle\sigma_{X,Y_{2}}\circ(1_{X}\otimes g)

\displaystyle=(g\otimes 1_{X})\circ\sigma_{X,Y_{1}}

for all
X,X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathcal{C},Y,Y_{1},Y_{2}\in\mathcal{D}
and

f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X_{1},X_{2}),g\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(Y_{1},Y_{2})
.
Often, the actions of a symmetric product of distinct monoidal categories on a given category demonstrate mutual commutativity.

Let
\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{+}}(z^{+},t^{+})\odot\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{-}}(z^{-},t^{-})
be the symmetric product
of
\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{+}}(z^{+},t^{+})
and
\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{-}}(z^{-},t^{-})
.
Diagrammatically, it is convenient to use
different colors,
denoting the
symmetric product
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{+}}(z^{+},t^{+})}\odot{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{-}}(z^{-},t^{-})}
and using the color
red (resp., blue) for objects and morphisms in
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{+}}(z^{+},t^{+})}
(resp.,
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{-}}(z^{-},t^{-})}
). For convenience, we call
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{+}}(z^{+},t^{+})}\odot{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{-}}(z^{-},t^{-})}

double quantum Heisenberg category
.
Morphisms may then be represented by linear combinations of string diagrams
colored both blue and red.
In fact, the double quantum Heisenberg category
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{+}}(z^{+},t^{+})}\odot{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{-}}(z^{-},t^{-})}
also has a definition by generators and relations as the following.

Theorem 1.4

(
[
32
]
)
.

The double quantum Heisenberg category
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{+}}(z^{+},t^{+})}\odot{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{-}}(z^{-},t^{-})}
is equivalent to the strict
R
-linear monoidal category
generated by the objects

F^{+}={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\uparrow},\quad E^{+}={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\downarrow},\quad F^{-}={\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\uparrow},\quad E^{-}={\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\downarrow},

and
morphisms
{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\bullet}\!\!\!\circ
,

1.5.
From Double quantum Heisenberg to
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
-categorification

Let
R
be a field and
\mathcal{C}
is a locally finite
R
-linear category. Similarly, a
categorical double quantum Heisenberg action
on a locally finite category
\mathcal{C}
is the data
of a strict monoidal functor
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{+}}(z^{+},t^{+})}\odot{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{-}}(z^{-},t^{-})}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}nd(\mathcal{C})
.
Now we assume that there exists a double quantum Heisenberg action
on a locally finite category
\mathcal{C}.

Similarly as in §
1.3
, for any irreducible object
L\in\mathcal{C},

we can define
m^{+}_{L}(u)\in R[u]
(resp.
n^{+}_{L}(u)\in R[u]
,
m^{-}_{L}(v)\in R[v]
and
n^{-}_{L}(v)\in R[v]
) to
be the monic
minimal polynomials
of
the endomorphisms

Let
I_{+}(q)
and
I_{-}(q)
be the quivers defined as in §
1.3
,
and write

\mathcal{K}_{q}:=I_{+}(q)\sqcup I_{-}(q)
for the quiver that is the disjoint union of
I_{+}(q)
and
I_{-}(q)
.
Notice that there is no arrow between
I_{+}(q)
and
I_{-}(q)
. In particular,

\mathcal{K}_{q}
is not connected. We may denote by

\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{\mathcal{K}_{q}}=\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
the corresponding Kac-Moody algebra which is a direct sum of
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}
and
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}.

We call the Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{\mathcal{K}_{q}}=\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
is
associated to the categorical action of
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{+}}(z^{+},t^{+})}\odot{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{H}eis_{k^{-}}(z^{-},t^{-})}
on
\mathcal{C}
.

Then the weight lattice of
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{\mathcal{K}_{q}}
is
X=X_{+}\times X_{-}
,
and fundamental weights are
\{\Lambda^{+}_{i}:=\Lambda_{i}\times 0\>|\>i\in I_{+}\}\sqcup\{\Lambda^{-}_{i^{\prime}}:=0\times\Lambda_{i^{\prime}}\>|\>i^{\prime}\in I_{-}\}
, etc.
For an irreducible object
L\in\mathcal{C}
, let

(1.29)

{\operatorname{wt}}(L):=\sum_{i\in I_{+}}(\phi^{+}_{i}(L)-\epsilon^{+}_{i}(L))\Lambda^{+}_{i}+\sum_{i^{\prime}\in I_{-}}(\phi^{-}_{i^{\prime}}(L)-\epsilon^{-}_{i^{\prime}}(L))\Lambda^{-}_{i^{\prime}}\in X.

Then for
\lambda\in X
we let
\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}
be the Serre
subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
consisting of the objects
V

such that every irreducible subquotient
L
of
V

satisfies
{\operatorname{wt}}(L)=\lambda
.
The point of this definition is
that irreducible objects
L,M\in\mathcal{C}
with
{\operatorname{wt}}(L)\neq{\operatorname{wt}}(M)

have different central characters.
Using also the general theory of blocks,
it is shown in
[
32
]
that

(1.30)

\textstyle\mathcal{C}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in X}\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}.

We call it the
weight space

decomposition of
\mathcal{C}
.

Theorem 1.5

(
[
32
]
)
.

Let
R
be a field.
Associated to
\mathcal{C}
,
there is a
2
-representation

\Phi:\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{K_{q}})\rightarrow\mathfrak{Cat}_{R}

defined on objects by

\lambda\mapsto\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}
,
on generating
1-morphisms by

E_{i}1_{\lambda}\mapsto E^{+}_{i}|_{\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}}

and
F_{i}1_{\lambda}\mapsto F^{+}_{i}|_{\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}}
for
i\in I_{+},
and
E_{j}1_{\lambda}\mapsto E^{-}_{j}|_{\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}}

and
F_{j}1_{\lambda}\mapsto F^{-}_{j}|_{\mathcal{C}_{\lambda}}
for
j\in I_{-}.

2.
Double quantum Heisenberg categorification for finite classical groups

Throughout this section, we always assume that
q
is a power of an odd prime,
\ell
is a prime with
\ell\nmid q(q-1)
,
K
is a field of characteristic 0,
\mathcal{O}
is a complete discrete valuation ring and
k
is a field of characteristic
\ell
. Let
R=K,

\mathcal{O}
or
k
.
We fix a square root
q^{1/2}
of
q
and a square root
\sqrt{-1}
of
-1
,
and we assume that
q^{1/2}
and
\sqrt{-1}
lie in
R
.
Let
\mathbf{G}_{n}
be one of
\mathbf{O}_{2n+1}
,

{\mathbf{Sp}}_{2n}
or
\mathbf{O}_{2n}
,
so that
G_{n}
is one of
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
,
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
or
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{\pm}(q)
.
As is conventional, we set
\mathbf{G}_{0}=G_{0}=\{1\}
, except in the
\mathbf{O}_{1}
case where

\mathbf{G}_{0}=G_{0}=\{\pm 1\}.
Let

\mathbb{N}^{*}=\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
in the

\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{-}(q)
case and
\mathbb{N}^{*}=\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
in all the other cases.
Define

RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits:=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}RG_{n}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits.

We also fix the following constants

(2.1)

\displaystyle z^{+}

\displaystyle=z^{-}=q^{1/2}-q^{-1/2},

(2.2)

\displaystyle t^{+}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\sqrt{-1}q^{-1/2}&\text{if $G_{n}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)$ or $\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)$ };\\
\sqrt{-1}&\text{if $G_{n}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)$},\end{cases}

(2.3)

\displaystyle t^{-}

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\sqrt{-1}q^{-1/2}&\text{if $G_{n}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)$};\\
\sqrt{-1}&\text{if $G_{n}=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)$ or $\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)$}.\end{cases}

2.1.
Categorical double quantum Heisenberg action

In this section, we will construct a
strict monoidal functor from a double quantum Heisenberg category to
\mathcal{E}nd(RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits)
.

2.1.1.
Construction of classical groups

For
n\geqslant 1
,
let
J_{n}
be the
n\times n
matrix with entry
1
in
(i,n-i+1)
for
1\leqslant i\leqslant n

and zero elsewhere, and denote
\widetilde{J}_{2n}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&J_{n}\\
-J_{n}&0\\
\end{array}\right)
.

(1) The odd-dimensional (full) orthogonal group
\mathbf{O}_{2n+1}

is

\mathbf{O}_{2n+1}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q})=\{g\in\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{2n+1}\,\mid\,{}^{t}gJ_{2n+1}g=J_{2n+1}\}.

The corresponding finite groups of fixed points under
F

are the
finite orthogonal group

\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
,
where
F
is the Frobenius endomorphism of
\mathbf{O}_{2n+1}
induced by
the standard Frobenius map
F_{q}
on
\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{2n+1}

raising all entries of a matrix to their
q
-th powers.

(2)
The symplectic group
{\mathbf{Sp}}_{2n}
is

{\mathbf{Sp}}_{2n}=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q})=\{g\in\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{2n}\,\mid\,{}^{t}g\widetilde{J}_{2n}g=\widetilde{J}_{2n}\},

and the
finite symplectic group

\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
is the finite group
({\mathbf{Sp}}_{2n})^{F}
of fixed points
of
{\mathbf{Sp}}_{2n}
under the Frobenius endomorphism
F
of
{\mathbf{Sp}}_{2n}

induced by the standard Frobenius map
F_{q}
on
\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{2n}
.

(3) The even-dimensional (full) orthogonal group
\mathbf{O}_{2n}
is

\mathbf{O}_{2n}=\mathrm{O}_{2n}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q})=\{g\in\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{2n}\,\mid\,{}^{t}gJ_{2n}g=J_{2n}\}.

(3a)

The
finite orthogonal group

\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{+}_{2n}(q)
is the group
(\mathbf{O}_{2n})^{F}
of fixed points
of
\mathbf{O}_{2n}
under the Frobenius endomorphism
F
of
\mathbf{O}_{2n}

induced by the standard Frobenius map
F_{q}
on
\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{2n}
.

(3b)

The
finite non-split orthogonal group

\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{-}_{2n}(q)
is
the group
(\mathbf{O}_{2n})^{F^{\prime}}
of fixed points of
\mathbf{O}_{2n}
under
F^{\prime}

where
F^{\prime}:=F_{q}\circ\sigma
and
\sigma(g)=sgs^{-1}

for
g\in\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{2n}
with
s=\ \operatorname{diag}\nolimits(\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-1},\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\
1&0\\
\end{array}\right),\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{{n-1}})\in\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{2n}
the permutation matrix
interchanging the
n
-th and
(n+1)
-th rows.

The groups
\mathbf{SO}_{2n+1}=\mathbf{O}_{2n+1}\cap\mathbf{SL}_{2n+1}
and
\mathbf{SO}_{2n}=\mathbf{O}_{2n+1}\cap\mathbf{SL}_{2n+1}
are known as special orthogonal groups, while their corresponding finite counterparts are referred to as finite special orthogonal groups, denoted
\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
and
\operatorname{SO}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
.

2.1.2.
Functors

In this subsection, we will recall the construction of functors defined in
[
39
, §4]
. For the sake of simplicity, we have simplified the subscripts for the definitions of functors in
[
39
, §4]
.

We first define the embedding of certain (possibly disconnected) Levi subgroups into
\mathbf{G}_{n}
.
Given
r,m,m_{1},m_{2},\dots,m_{t}\in\mathbb{N}
such that
m=\sum_{i}m_{i}
and
n=r+m
,
we always embed the group
\mathbf{G}_{r}\times\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{m_{1}}\times\dots\times\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{m_{t}}
into
\mathbf{G}_{n}
via the map:

\displaystyle\mathbf{G}_{r}\times\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{m_{1}}\times\dots\times\mathbf{G}\mathbf{L}_{m_{t}}

\displaystyle\hookrightarrow\mathbf{G}_{n}

\displaystyle B\times A_{1}\times\dots\times A_{t}

\displaystyle\mapsto{\rm diag}(A_{t},\ldots,A_{1},B,A_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,A_{t}^{\prime})

where

A_{i}^{\prime}=J_{m_{i}}A_{i}^{-tr}J_{m_{i}}
.
The image of the above map, which is a Levi subgroup of
\mathbf{G}_{n}
, will be denoted by

\mathbf{L}_{r,m_{1},\dots,m_{t}}
. The corresponding Levi subgroup of
G_{n}

will be denoted by
L_{r,m_{1},\dots,m_{t}}
.
In particular, the finite group corresponding to
\mathbf{L}_{r,1^{m}}

is
L_{r,1^{m}}\simeq G_{r}\times\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{1}(q)^{m}
.

The subgroup of upper-triangular matrices
\mathbf{B}_{r+1}
in
\mathbf{G}_{r+1}
is a Borel subgroup.
Let
\mathbf{P}_{r}
be the parabolic subgroup of
\mathbf{G}_{r+1}
containing
\mathbf{B}_{r+1}
with the Levi complement
\mathbf{L}_{r,1}.

We write
P_{r}=\mathbf{P}_{r}^{F}
(or
\mathbf{P}_{r}^{F^{\prime}}
in the case of
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2r}^{-}(q)
).
Let
\mathbf{V}_{r}
be the unipotent radical of
\mathbf{P}_{r}
and
V_{r}=\mathbf{V}_{r}^{F}
(or
\mathbf{V}_{r}^{F^{\prime}}
in the case of
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2r}^{-}(q)
),
and
U_{r}\subset G_{r+1}
be the subgroup given by

(2.4)

\displaystyle U_{r}=\mathbb{F}^{\times}_{q}\ltimes V_{r}=\begin{pmatrix}*&*&\cdots&\cdots&*\\
&1&&(0)&\vdots\\
&&\ddots&&\vdots\\
&(0)&&1&*\\
&&&&*\end{pmatrix},

where we identify
\mathbb{F}^{\times}_{q}
with
\{{\rm diag}(t,1,\ldots,1,t^{-1})\in U_{r}\mid t\in\mathbb{F}^{\times}_{q}\}.
So we have
P_{r}=G_{r}\ltimes U_{r}
and
P_{r}=L_{r,1}\ltimes V_{r}.

Remark 2.1
.

More precisely,
\mathbf{V}_{r}
consists of all matrices of the form

\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&-v_{1}^{tr}J_{2r+1}&-\frac{v_{1}^{tr}J_{2r+1}v_{1}}{2}\\
&\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{\mathbf{G}_{r}}&v_{1}\\
&&1\\
\end{array}\right),\>\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&v_{2}^{tr}\widetilde{J}_{2r}&z\\
&\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{\mathbf{G}_{r}}&v_{2}\\
&&1\\
\end{array}\right),\>\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&-v^{tr}J_{2r}&-\frac{v_{3}^{tr}J_{2r}v_{3}}{2}\\
&\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{\mathbf{G}_{r}}&v_{3}\\
&&1\\
\end{array}\right)

where
z\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q},

v_{1}\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{2r+1}
and
v_{2},v_{3}\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{2r},
and
\mathbf{G}_{r}=\mathbf{O}_{2r+1},{\mathbf{Sp}}_{2r}
or
\mathbf{O}_{2r}
, respectively.
In particular, the order
|V_{r}|
of
V_{r}=\mathbf{V}_{r}^{F}
(or
\mathbf{V}_{r}^{F^{\prime}}
in the case of
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2r}^{-}(q)
) is equal to
q^{2r+1},q^{2r+1}
or
q^{2r}
when
G_{r}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2r+1}(q),\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2r}(q)
or
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2r}^{\pm}(q)
, respectively.

Since
\mathbb{F}^{\times}_{q}
is a cyclic group of order
q-1
and
q
is odd,
we denote by
\zeta
the unique character of order 2 (Legendre symbol for
\mathbb{F}^{\times}_{q}
) and view it as a character of
U_{r}
via the surjection
U_{r}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{F}^{\times}_{q}
.
Now we define two idempotents of
RP_{r}:

e^{+}_{r}:=e_{U_{r}}=\frac{1}{|U_{r}|}\sum_{u\in U_{r}}u,

and

e^{-}_{r}:=\frac{1}{|U_{r}|}\sum_{u\in U_{r}}\zeta(u^{-1})u.

The idempotents defined above satisfy the following:

•

for any
u\in U_{r},ue^{+}_{r}=e^{+}_{r}u=e^{+}_{r}
and
ue^{-}_{r}=e^{-}_{r}u=\zeta(u)e^{-}_{r};

•

for any
g\in G_{r},ge^{+}_{r}=e^{+}_{r}g=e^{+}_{r}
and
ge^{-}_{r}=e^{-}_{r}g=e^{-}_{r}.

From now on, we identify
e^{\pm}_{r}
with its image in
RG_{n}

under the embedding
\iota_{r,n}:G_{r}\to G_{n}.

The
(RG_{r+1},RG_{r})
-bimodules
RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r}
and

RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}
are both left
RG_{r+1}
-projective
and right
RG_{r}
-projective, so we can define
the following bi-adjoint functors
(F_{r,r+1}^{+},E_{r+1,r}^{+})
and
(F_{r,r+1}^{-},E_{r+1,r}^{-})
(see
[
39
, §4]
, see also
[
19
, §6.2]
):

\begin{array}[]{rcrclcl}F^{+}_{r,r+1}&=&RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}-&:&\,RG_{r}\operatorname{-mod}&\to&RG_{r+1}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits,\\
E^{+}_{r+1,r}&=&e^{+}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\otimes_{RG_{r+1}}-&:&\,RG_{r+1}\operatorname{-mod}&\to&RG_{r}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits,\\
F^{-}_{r,r+1}&=&RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}-&:&\,RG_{r}\operatorname{-mod}&\to&RG_{r+1}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits,\\
E^{-}_{r+1,r}&=&e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\otimes_{RG_{r+1}}-&:&\,RG_{r+1}\operatorname{-mod}&\to&RG_{r}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits.\end{array}

For
M\in RG_{r}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
, we have

(2.5)

\displaystyle F^{+}_{r,r+1}(M)\cong R_{L_{r,1}}^{G_{r+1}}(M\boxtimes R_{1})~\mbox{and}~F^{-}_{r,r+1}(M)\cong R_{L_{r,1}}^{G_{r+1}}(M\boxtimes R_{\zeta}),

where
R_{L_{r,1}}^{G_{r+1}}
is the Harish-Chandra induction functor,
R_{1}
and
R_{\zeta}
are the
R\mathbb{F}^{\times}_{q}
-modules
affording the trivial character of
\mathbb{F}^{\times}_{q}
and
the Legendre symbol
\zeta
, respectively.

Now we set

F^{+}=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}F^{+}_{r,r+1},\qquad E^{+}=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}E^{+}_{r+1,r},

F^{-}=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}F^{-}_{r,r+1},\qquad E^{-}=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}E^{-}_{r+1,r}.

Then these functors define endo-functors of category
RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits.

Diagrammatically, it is convenient to use the color red for the functors
E^{+}
,
F^{+}
and use the color blue for
E^{-}
,
F^{-}.

2.1.3.
Adjunctions

Since
(E^{+},F^{+})
and
(E^{-},F^{-})
are bi-adjoint pairs, there exist four adjunction maps for each pair. Note that they are unique up to a scalar.
Now we give explicit constructions of these adjunction maps by using the corresponding bimodule maps as follows.

(a)

For an element
a\in G_{r+1}
, we set

\mathrm{Proj}^{\pm}_{P_{r}}(e^{\pm}_{r}ae^{\pm}_{r})=\begin{cases}e^{\pm}_{r}ae^{\pm}_{r}\,\,&\text{if}\,\,a\in P_{r},\\
0\,\,&\text{if}\,\,a\notin P_{r}.\end{cases}

Extending by
R
-linearity, this defines
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule
maps

\varepsilon^{\pm}_{L}:e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\to e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot P_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\cong RG_{r}.

The second
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodules isomorphism
e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RP_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\cong RG_{r}
is determined by sending
e^{\pm}_{r}
to
1\in RG_{r}.

(b)

Let
G_{r}=\coprod\limits_{i=1}^{s}P_{r-1}g_{i}
be a decomposition of
G_{r}
into left
P_{r-1}
cosets. The elements

Z^{\pm}_{r}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{s}(g_{i}^{-1}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}g_{i})\in RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}

do not depend on the choice of representatives
\{g_{i}\}_{i=1}^{s}
and satisfies
aZ^{\pm}_{r}=Z^{\pm}_{r}a
for any
a\in G_{r}
.

Then we define
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule maps as follows:

\eta^{\pm}_{L}:RG_{r}\to RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r},\quad a\mapsto aZ^{\pm}_{r}=Z^{\pm}_{r}a

for any
a\in RG_{r}.

(c)

We define by
\varepsilon^{\pm}_{R}
the following
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule maps:

\varepsilon^{\pm}_{R}:RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}\to RG_{r},\quad ge^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}h\mapsto-t^{\pm}z^{\pm}ge^{\pm}_{r-1}h,

for any
g,h\in RG_{r}
. Note that
t^{\pm}
and
z^{\pm}
are constants defined in (
2.1
), (
2.2
) and (
2.3
).

(d)

Finally we define by
\eta^{\pm}_{R}
the following
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule maps:

\eta^{\pm}_{R}:RG_{r}\to e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r},\quad g\mapsto-(t^{\pm}z^{\pm})^{-1}ge^{\pm}_{r}

for all
g\in RG_{r}.

2.1.4.
Lifts of simple reflections

Let
\mathbf{G}_{n}
be one of
\mathbf{O}_{2n+1}
,
{\mathbf{Sp}}_{2n}
or
\mathbf{O}_{2n}
.
Let
\mathbf{T}
be the split maximal torus consisting of diagonal matrices of the connected component
\mathbf{G}_{n}^{\circ}

of
\mathbf{G}_{n}
. The group
W_{n}:=N_{\mathbf{G}_{n}}(\mathbf{T})/C_{\mathbf{G}_{n}}(\mathbf{T})
is a Weyl group of
type
B_{n}.

The numbering of the simple reflections of
W_{n}
will be taken
the following convention:

(2.6)

When
\mathbf{G}_{n}=\mathbf{O}_{2n+1},
we have

\mathbf{T}=\{{\rm diag}(t_{n},\ldots,t_{1},1,t_{1}^{-1},\ldots,t_{n}^{-1})\mid t_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{\times}~\text{for~all}\\
1\leqslant i\leqslant n\}.
It is easy to see that
\widehat{\mathbf{T}}=C_{\mathbf{G}_{n}}(\mathbf{T})=\{{\rm diag}(t_{n},\ldots,t_{1},\pm 1,t_{1}^{-1},\ldots,t_{n}^{-1})\mid t_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{\times}~\text{for~all}~1\leqslant i\leqslant n\}
and
W_{n}\cong N_{\mathbf{G}^{\circ}_{n}}(\mathbf{T})/\mathbf{T}
is a Weyl group of
type
B_{n}
on which
F
acts trivially.
For
i\neq 1
, the simple
reflection
s_{i}
can be lifted to
N_{\mathbf{G}_{n}}(\mathbf{T})
as the signed permutation matrix

\dot{s}_{i}=\ \operatorname{diag}\nolimits(\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-i},\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\
-1&0\\
\end{array}\right),\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{\mathbf{G}_{i-2}},\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&-1\\
1&0\\
\end{array}\right),\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-i})
and
s_{1}

is lifted to be the signed permutation matrix

\dot{s}_{1}=\ \begin{array}[]{(ccc|ccc|ccc)}\BAmulticolumn{3}{c|}{\hbox{\multirowsetup$\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-1}$}}&&&&&&\\
&&&&&&&&&\\
\cline{1-9}\cr&&&0&0&-1&&&&\\
&&&0&1&0&&&&\\
&&&-1&0&0&&&&\\
\cline{1-9}\cr&&&&&&\BAmulticolumn{3}{c}{\hbox{\multirowsetup$\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-1}$}}\\
&&&&&&&&&\\
\end{array}\,\,.

When
\mathbf{G}_{n}={\mathbf{Sp}}_{2n}
, we have
\mathbf{T}=\{\mathrm{diag}(t_{n},\ldots,t_{1},t_{1}^{-1},\ldots,t_{n}^{-1})\mid t_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{\times}
for all
1\leqslant i\leqslant n\}
.
Similarly,
the simple reflection
s_{i}(i>1)
can be lifted to
N_{\mathbf{G}_{n}}(\mathbf{T})
as the signed permutation matrix

\dot{s}_{i}=\ \operatorname{diag}\nolimits(\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-i},\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\
-1&0\\
\end{array}\right),\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{\mathbf{G}_{i-2}},\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&-1\\
1&0\\
\end{array}\right),\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-i})
and
s_{1}
as the signed permutation matrix

\dot{s}_{1}=\ \begin{array}[]{(cccc|cc|cccc)}\BAmulticolumn{4}{c|}{\hbox{\multirowsetup$\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-1}$}}&&&&&\\
&&&&&&&&&\\
\cline{1-10}\cr&&&&0&-1&&&&\\
&&&&1&0&&&&\\
\cline{1-10}\cr&&&&&&\BAmulticolumn{3}{c}{\hbox{\multirowsetup$\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-1}$}}\\
&&&&&&&&&\end{array}\ .

When
\mathbf{G}_{n}=\mathbf{O}_{2n}
, we have
\mathbf{T}=\{\mathrm{diag}(t_{n},\ldots,t_{1},t_{1}^{-1},\ldots,t_{n}^{-1})\mid t_{i}\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{\times}
for all
1\leqslant i\leqslant n\}
.

For
i\neq 1
, the simple
reflection
s_{i}
can be lifted to
N_{\mathbf{G}_{n}}(\mathbf{T})
as the signed permutation matrix

\dot{s}_{i}=\ \operatorname{diag}\nolimits(\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-i},\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\
-1&0\\
\end{array}\right),\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{\mathbf{G}_{i-2}},\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&-1\\
1&0\\
\end{array}\right),\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-i})
and
s_{1}
as the signed permutation matrix

\dot{s}_{1}=\ \begin{array}[]{(cccc|cc|cccc)}\BAmulticolumn{4}{c|}{\hbox{\multirowsetup$\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-1}$}}&&&&&\\
&&&&&&&&&\\
\cline{1-10}\cr&&&&0&-1&&&&\\
&&&&-1&0&&&&\\
\cline{1-10}\cr&&&&&&\BAmulticolumn{3}{c}{\hbox{\multirowsetup$\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{n-1}$}}\\
&&&&&&&&&\end{array}\ .

For the next section,
we now define

x_{1}:=s_{1}
and

x_{k}:=s_{k}s_{k-1}\cdots s_{2}x_{1}s_{2}^{-1}\cdots s^{-1}_{k-1}s^{-1}_{k}\,\,\text{for}\,\,2\leqslant k\leqslant n.

Correspondingly, we define their lifts by
\dot{x}_{1}=\dot{s}_{1}
and

\dot{x}_{k}:=\dot{s}_{k}\dot{s}_{k-1}\cdots\dot{s}_{2}\dot{x}_{1}\dot{s}_{2}^{-1}\cdots\dot{s}^{-1}_{k-1}\dot{s}^{-1}_{k}\,\,\text{for}\,\,2\leqslant k\leqslant n.

2.1.5.
Natural transformations

In this subsection, we will recall the construction of some natural transformations appearing in
[
39
, §4.2.2]
, see also
[
19
, §6.2]
.

An endomorphism of
F^{\pm}_{r,r+1}
can be represented by an
(RG_{r+1},RG_{r})
-bimodule endomorphism of
RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}
, or equivalently, by right multiplication by an element of
e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}
centralizing
G_{r}
.
It is easy to show that
e_{r+1}^{\epsilon}e_{r}^{\epsilon^{\prime}}=e_{r}^{\epsilon^{\prime}}e_{r+1}^{\epsilon}
for any
\epsilon,\epsilon^{\prime}\in\{\pm\},
so
e_{r+1}^{\epsilon}e_{r}^{\epsilon^{\prime}}
is an idempotent.
The functors
F^{+}_{r+1,r+2}F^{+}_{r,r+1},

F^{-}_{r+1,r+2}F^{-}_{r,r+1},

F^{+}_{r+1,r+2}F^{-}_{r,r+1}
and
F^{-}_{r+1,r+2}F^{+}_{r,r+1}

are
represented by the
(RG_{r+2},RG_{r})
-bimodules

RG_{r+2}\cdot e^{+}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r},\ \ RG_{r+2}\cdot e^{-}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r},\ \ RG_{r+2}\cdot e^{+}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r},\ \ RG_{r+2}\cdot e^{-}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r},

respectively. An endomorphism of those functors can be represented by right multiplication by an element of

e^{+}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+2}\cdot e^{+}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r},\ \ e^{-}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+2}\cdot e^{-}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r},

e^{+}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+2}\cdot e^{+}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r},\ \ e^{-}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+2}\cdot e^{-}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}

centralizing
RG_{r}
, respectively.
Let
\dot{x}_{r+1}
and
\dot{s}_{r+2}
be as defined in §
2.1.4
.
It is easy to see that both
\dot{x}_{r+1}\in G_{r+1}
and
\dot{s}_{r+2}\in G_{r+2}
centralize
G_{r}
.
In fact,

\dot{x}_{r+1}

is exactly the matrix

\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}&&-1\\
&\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{G_{r}}&\\
-1\\
\end{array}\right),\quad\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}&&-1\\
&\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{G_{r}}&\\
\,1\\
\end{array}\right)\quad\text{or}\quad\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}&&-1\\
&\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{G_{r}}&\\
-1\\
\end{array}\right)

when
G_{n}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q),\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
or
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{\pm}(q)
, respectively.

Thus, the right multiplication by the elements

\displaystyle X^{+}_{r+1}=q^{r}e^{+}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}\,e^{+}_{r},\qquad X^{-}_{r+1}=\beta q^{r}e^{-}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}\,e^{-}_{r},

define natural transformations of the functors
F^{+}_{r}
and
F^{-}_{r}
, respectively,
where

(2.7)

\displaystyle\beta=\begin{cases}\sqrt{\zeta(-1)}q^{-1/2}\quad\text{if $G_{n}=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)$};\\
\zeta(2)\quad\text{if $G_{n}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)$ or $\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)$}\end{cases}

which is a normalization.
Similarly, the right multiplication by the elements

\displaystyle T^{+}_{r+2}=q^{1/2}e^{+}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+2}\,e^{+}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}\,,\ \ H_{r+2}=q^{1/2}e^{+}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+2}\,e^{-}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}\,,

\displaystyle T^{-}_{r+2}=q^{1/2}e^{-}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+2}\,e^{-}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\,,\ \ H^{\prime}_{r+2}=q^{1/2}e^{-}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+2}\,e^{+}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\,,

define natural transformations in

\displaystyle{\operatorname{End}}(F^{+}_{r+1,r+2}F^{+}_{r,r+1})\,,\operatorname{Hom}(F^{+}_{r+1,r+2}F^{-}_{r,r+1},F^{-}_{r+1,r+2}F^{+}_{r,r+1})\,,

\displaystyle{\operatorname{End}}(F^{-}_{r+1,r+2}F^{-}_{r,r+1})\,,\operatorname{Hom}(F^{-}_{r+1,r+2}F^{+}_{r,r+1},F^{+}_{r+1,r+2}F^{-}_{r,r+1})\,,

respectively.

Remark 2.2
.

Note that in this article, we use slightly different notations and choose a different normalization with
[
39
]
to define these natural transformations.

We set

X^{+}=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}X^{+}_{r+1}\,,\qquad X^{-}=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}X^{-}_{r+1}\,,\qquad T^{+}=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}T^{+}_{r+2}\,,

T^{-}=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}T^{-}_{r+2}\,,\qquad H=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}H_{r+2}\,,\qquad H^{\prime}=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb{N}^{*}}H^{\prime}_{r+2}\,.

2.1.6.

.

There is a unique strict
R

\Psi

sends the generating morphisms to the corresponding natural transformations

RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits

2.1.7.
Categorical Kac-Moody action

Let
{I}_{+}
(resp.
{I}_{-}
) be the set of the generalized eigenvalues of
X^{+}
on
F^{+}
(resp.
X^{-}
on
F^{-}
).
We have the decompositions

E^{+}=\bigoplus_{i\in I_{+}}E^{+}_{i},\ \ \ \ F^{+}=\bigoplus_{i\in I_{+}}F^{+}_{i},\ \ \ \ E^{-}=\bigoplus_{i^{\prime}\in I_{-}}E^{-}_{i^{\prime}},\ \ \ \ F^{-}=\bigoplus_{i^{\prime}\in I_{-}}F^{-}_{i^{\prime}}

such that
X^{+}-i
is locally nilpotent on
E^{+}_{i}
and
F^{+}_{i}
and
X^{-}-i^{\prime}
is locally nilpotent on
E^{-}_{i^{\prime}}
and
F^{-}_{i^{\prime}}
,
respectively. As a direct consequence of Theorem
2.3
and
Theorem
1.5
, we have the following theorem. The set
I_{+}
and
I_{-}
will be determined in Proposition
4.9
.

Theorem 2.4
.

Let
R=K
or
k
and assume
\ell\nmid q(q-1).

Then there exists a
\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}})
-categorification on
RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
, i.e., there is a strict
R
-linear monoidal functor

\Psi^{\prime}:\,\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}})\to\mathcal{E}nd(RG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits).

2.2.
The proof of the main theorem

In this section, we start to check all the relations in Theorem
2.3
. Most relations are checked by explicit computations and the most interesting one is to check the invertibility of
X^{+}
and
X^{-}
, which is given in §
2.2.8
.

2.2.1.
Double cosets decomposition

Lemma 2.5
.

(a)

The set
D_{r,r}
of the distinguished representatives for double coset
W_{r}\backslash W_{r+1}/W_{r}
is
\{1,x_{r+1},s_{r+1}\}.

(b)

The double coset
P_{r}\backslash G_{r+1}/P_{r}
are exactly
\{P_{r},P_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}P_{r},P_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}P_{r}\}.

(c)

G_{r}\cap{{}^{s_{r+1}}P}_{r}=P_{r-1}.

(d)

{}^{s_{r+1}}U_{r-1}\leq U_{r}.

Proof.

They are easy to check by direct computations.
∎

Lemma 2.6
.

We have

e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}=e^{+}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1}\,,\quad e^{-}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}=e^{-}_{r}e^{-}_{r-1}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}e^{-}_{r-1}\,,

e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}=e^{+}_{r}e^{-}_{r-1}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1}\,,\quad e^{-}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}=e^{-}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}e^{-}_{r-1}.

Proof.

We only prove
e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}=e^{+}_{r}e^{-}_{r-1}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1}
. The others are similar.
By definition we have
e^{+}_{r}=\frac{1}{|U_{r}|}\sum\limits_{g\in U_{r}}g
and
e^{-}_{r}=\frac{1}{|U_{r}|}\sum\limits_{g\in U_{r}}\zeta(g^{-1})g.

On the other hand, by Lemma
2.5
(d)
, we have
{}^{s_{r+1}}U_{r-1}\subset U_{r}
, so
{}^{s_{r+1}}{e^{\pm}_{r-1}}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}=e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot^{s_{r+1}}{e^{\pm}_{r-1}}=e^{\pm}_{r}.

By moving
e^{-}_{r-1}
to the right, we get

\displaystyle e^{+}_{r}e^{-}_{r-1}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1}=

\displaystyle e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}{{}^{{s}_{r+1}}e^{-}_{r-1}}e^{-}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1}

since
{}^{s_{r+1}}{e^{-}_{r-1}}\cdot e^{-}_{r}=e^{-}_{r}.

By moving
e^{+}_{r-1}
to the left, we get

\displaystyle e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1}=

\displaystyle e^{+}_{r}(^{{s}_{r+1}}e^{+}_{r-1}\dot{s}_{r+1})e^{-}_{r}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}

where the last equation is deduced from
e^{+}_{r}\cdot(^{s_{r+1}}{e^{+}_{r-1}})=e^{+}_{r}
. So the lemma follows.
∎

Proposition 2.7
.

(a)

As an
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule,
e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}
is generated by
e^{\pm}_{r}\,,X^{\pm}_{r+1}
and
T^{\pm}_{r+1}.

Moreover, We have the following
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule isomorphism

(2.13)

\displaystyle e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\cong RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\oplus RG_{r}\cdot X^{\pm}_{r+1}\oplus RG_{r}\cdot T^{\pm}_{r+1}\cdot RG_{r}.

(b)

As
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodules,
e^{+}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}
is generated by
H_{r+1}
and
e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r}
is generated by
H^{\prime}_{r+1},

equivalently, we have the following
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule isomorphisms

(2.14)

\displaystyle e^{+}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}\cong RG_{r}\cdot H_{r+1}\cdot RG_{r}

and

(2.15)

\displaystyle e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r}\cong RG_{r}\cdot H^{\prime}_{r+1}\cdot RG_{r}.

Proof.

(a)
By Lemma
2.5
(b)
, we have

G_{r+1}=P_{r}\sqcup P_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}P_{r}\sqcup P_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}P_{r}.

It is obviously
(L_{r,1},L_{r,1})
-equivariant. So we have the following
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule decomposition

e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}=e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RP_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\oplus e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot R(P_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}P_{r})\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\oplus e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot R(P_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}P_{r})\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}.

Since
e^{\pm}_{r}
commutes with
G_{r}
and
\dot{x}_{r+1}
commutes with
G_{r}
, we have

e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RP_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}=RP_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}=e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RP_{r}=RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}

and

e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot R(P_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}P_{r})\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}=RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{\pm}_{r}=RG_{r}\cdot(ce^{\pm}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{\pm}_{r})=RG_{r}\cdot X^{\pm}_{r+1}

where
c
is any non-zero constant.

Now we prove
e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot R(P_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}P_{r})\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}=RG_{r}\cdot T^{\pm}_{r+1}\cdot RG_{r}.

Note that

e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot R(P_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}P_{r})\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}=RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r},

which is equal to
RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{\pm}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}=RG_{r}\cdot T^{\pm}_{r+1}\cdot RG_{r}
by Lemma
2.6
.

(b)
Similarly, we have the following
(G_{r},G_{r})
-bimodule decomposition

e^{+}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}=e^{+}_{r}\cdot RP_{r}\cdot e^{-}_{r}\oplus e^{+}_{r}\cdot R(P_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}P_{r})\cdot e^{-}_{r}\oplus e^{+}_{r}\cdot R(P_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}P_{r})\cdot e^{-}_{r}.

Note that
e^{+}_{r}
commutes with
G_{r}
and
\dot{x}_{r+1}
commutes with
G_{r}
, so we have

e^{+}_{r}\cdot RP_{r}\cdot e^{-}_{r}=RP_{r}\cdot e^{+}_{r}e^{-}_{r}=0

where the last equation follows from the orthogonality of
e^{+}_{r}
and
e^{-}_{r}.

Similarly, we have

e^{+}_{r}\cdot R(P_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}P_{r})\cdot e^{-}_{r}=RG_{r}\cdot e^{+}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}=RG_{r}\cdot\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}e^{-}_{r}=0.

So we have

e^{+}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}=e^{+}_{r}\cdot R(P_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}P_{r})\cdot e^{-}_{r},
and by a similar argument as in
(a)
, we get

e^{+}_{r}\cdot R(P_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}P_{r})\cdot e^{-}_{r}=RG_{r}\cdot e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r}=RG_{r}\cdot H_{r+1}\cdot RG_{r}\,.

The same proof works for
e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r}\cong RG_{r}\cdot H^{\prime}_{r+1}\cdot RG_{r}.

∎

Remark 2.8
.

Note that the maps
\varepsilon^{\pm}_{L}:e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\to RG_{r+1}
defined in §1.1.2 coincide with the projections to the first
direct summand.

2.2.3.
Adjunctions

Proposition 2.10
.

The maps
\varepsilon^{\pm}_{R}
,
\eta^{\pm}_{R}
,
\varepsilon^{\pm}_{L}
,
\eta^{\pm}_{L}
defined above make
(E^{\pm},F^{\pm})
into a biadjoint pair, i.e., the natural transformations satisfy the relations
(\ref{adj})
for both red color and blue color.

Proof.

Note that the functors
F^{+},F^{-}
are special cases of parabolic induction functors and the functors
E^{+},E^{-}
are special cases of parabolic restriction functors defined in
[
41
, §7]
. The proof is deduced from
[
41
, Proposition 7.5]
.
∎

By the definition,
\mathrm{RH}=(1_{E^{+}}\otimes 1_{F^{-}}\otimes\varepsilon^{+}_{R})\circ(1_{E^{+}}\otimes H\otimes 1_{E^{+}})\circ(\eta^{+}_{R}\otimes 1_{F^{-}}\otimes 1_{E^{+}})

and
\mathrm{RH}^{\prime}=(1_{E^{-}}\otimes 1_{F^{+}}\otimes\varepsilon^{-}_{R})\circ(1_{E^{-}}\otimes H^{\prime}\otimes 1_{E^{-}})\circ(\eta^{-}_{R}\otimes 1_{F^{+}}\otimes 1_{E^{-}})
.

Lemma 2.11
.

(a)

The natural transformations
\mathrm{RT}^{\pm}:F^{\pm}_{r-1,r}E^{\pm}_{r,r-1}\Rightarrow E^{\pm}_{r+1,r}F^{\pm}_{r,r+1}
are given by the
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule map

RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}\to e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r},

ae^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}b\mapsto e^{\pm}_{r}aT_{r+1}be^{\pm}_{r}

for any
a,b\in G_{r}.

(b)

\mathrm{RH}:F^{+}_{r-1,r}E^{-}_{r,r-1}\Rightarrow E^{-}_{r+1,r}F^{+}_{r,r+1}
is given by the
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule map

RG_{r}\cdot e^{+}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{-}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}\to e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r},

ae^{+}_{r-1}\otimes e^{-}_{r-1}b\mapsto e^{-}_{r}aH_{r+1}be^{+}_{r}

and
\mathrm{RH}^{\prime}:F^{-}_{r-1,r}E^{+}_{r,r-1}\Rightarrow E^{+}_{r+1,r}F^{-}_{r,r+1}
is given by the
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule map

RG_{r}\cdot e^{-}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{+}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}\to e^{+}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}

ae^{-}_{r-1}\otimes e^{+}_{r-1}b\mapsto e^{+}_{r}aH^{\prime}_{r+1}be^{-}_{r}

for any
a,b\in G_{r}.

Proof.

We only prove
(a)
and the proof of
(b)
is similar. As an
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule, the module
RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}
is generated by the unique element
e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}
, so we only need to compute the image of it. Note that
\mathrm{RT}^{\pm}_{r}
is the composition of the following bimodule maps:

\displaystyle RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}\cong RG_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eta^{\pm}_{R}\otimes 1\otimes 1}}{{\longrightarrow}}e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\otimes_{RG_{r+1}}RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}\cdot e^{-}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 1\otimes T^{\pm}\otimes 1}}{{\longrightarrow}}e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\otimes_{RG_{r+1}}RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 1\otimes 1\otimes\varepsilon^{\pm}_{R}}}{{\longrightarrow}}e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\otimes_{RG_{r+1}}RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}\cong e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}.

We compute the image of
e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}
as follows:

\displaystyle e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}\xrightarrow{\thicksim}1\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}

\displaystyle\mapsto-(t^{\pm}z^{\pm})^{-1}e^{\pm}_{r}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}

\displaystyle\mapsto-(t^{\pm}z^{\pm})^{-1}e^{\pm}_{r}\otimes T^{\pm}_{r+1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}

\displaystyle\mapsto e^{\pm}_{r}\otimes T^{\pm}_{r+1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}\xrightarrow{\thicksim}e^{\pm}_{r}T^{\pm}_{r+1}e^{\pm}_{r-1}=T^{\pm}_{r+1}.

∎

By the definition,
\mathrm{LH}=(\varepsilon^{-}_{L}\otimes 1_{F^{+}}\otimes 1_{E^{-}})\circ(1_{E^{-}}\otimes H\otimes 1_{E^{-}})\circ(1_{E^{-}}\otimes 1_{F^{+}}\otimes\eta^{-}_{L})
and
\mathrm{LH}^{\prime}=(\varepsilon^{+}_{L}\otimes 1_{F^{-}}\otimes 1_{E^{+}})\circ(1_{E^{+}}\otimes H^{\prime}\otimes 1_{E^{+}})\circ(1_{E^{+}}\otimes 1_{F^{-}}\otimes\eta^{+}_{L}).

Lemma 2.12
.

(a)

The natural transformation
\mathrm{LT}^{\pm}:E^{\pm}_{r+1,r}F^{\pm}_{r,r+1}\Rightarrow F^{\pm}_{r-1,r}E^{\pm}_{r,r-1}
is given by the
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule map

e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\to RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}

e^{\pm}_{r}\mapsto 0,

X^{\pm}_{r+1}\mapsto 0,

T^{\pm}_{r+1}\mapsto e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}.

(b)

The natural transformation
\mathrm{LH}:E^{-}_{r,r-1}F^{+}_{r,r+1}\Rightarrow F^{+}_{r-1,r}E^{-}_{r,r-1}
is given by the
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule map

e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r}\to RG_{r}\cdot e^{+}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{-}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r},

H^{\prime}_{r+1}\mapsto e^{+}_{r-1}\otimes e^{-}_{r-1},

and the natural transformation
\mathrm{LH}^{\prime}:E^{+}_{r+1,r}F^{-}_{r,r+1}\Rightarrow F^{-}_{r,r-1}E^{+}_{r-1,r}
is given by the
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule map

e^{+}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}\to RG_{r}\cdot e^{-}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{+}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r},

H_{r+1}\mapsto e^{-}_{r-1}\otimes e^{+}_{r-1}.

Proof.

Let
G_{r}=\coprod\limits_{i=1}^{s}P_{r-1}g_{i}
be a decomposition of
G_{r}
into left
P_{r-1}
cosets.

(a)

\mathrm{RT}^{\pm}
is the composition of the following bimodule maps:

\displaystyle e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\cong e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 1\otimes 1\otimes\eta^{\pm}_{L}}}{{\longrightarrow}}e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 1\otimes T^{\pm}\otimes 1}}{{\longrightarrow}}e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\varepsilon^{\pm}_{L}\otimes 1\otimes 1}}{{\longrightarrow}}RG_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}\cong RG_{r}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}.

We compute the image of
y\in e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}
:

\displaystyle y\xrightarrow{\thicksim}y\otimes 1

\displaystyle\mapsto y\otimes Z^{\pm}_{r}=y\otimes(\sum\limits_{i=1}^{s}g_{i}^{-1}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}g_{i})

\displaystyle\mapsto y\otimes\sum\limits_{i=1}^{s}(g_{i}^{-1}T^{\pm}_{r+1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}g_{i})

\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{s}(yg_{i}^{-1}T^{\pm}_{r+1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}g_{i})

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum\limits_{i=1}^{s}(\mathrm{Proj}^{\pm}_{P_{r}}(yg^{-1}_{i}T^{\pm}_{r+1})\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}g_{i})\,.

Let
y=e^{\pm}_{r}.
For any
g_{i}\in G_{r},

g^{-1}_{i}\dot{s}_{r+1}\notin P_{r}
, we have
\mathrm{Proj}^{\pm}_{P_{r}}(e^{\pm}_{r}g^{-1}_{i}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{\pm}_{r})=0
.
Hence
e^{\pm}_{r}\mapsto 0.

Let
y=X^{\pm}_{r+1}.

For any
h\in G_{r},

we have

\displaystyle X^{\pm}_{r+1}hT^{\pm}_{r+1}=hX^{\pm}_{r+1}T^{\pm}_{r+1}

\displaystyle=hT^{\pm}_{r+1}X^{\pm}_{r}T^{\pm}_{r+1}T^{\pm}_{r+1}\quad\text{(by Prop.\ref{prop:12relations} $(\ref{AHH1})$ and $(\ref{AHH2})$)}

\displaystyle=hT^{\pm}_{r+1}X^{\pm}_{r}(z^{\pm}T^{\pm}_{r+1}+e^{\pm}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r-1})\quad\text{(by Prop.\ref{prop:12relations} $(\ref{AHH1})$)}

\displaystyle=z^{\pm}hX^{\pm}_{r+1}+hT^{\pm}_{r+1}X^{\pm}_{r}\quad\text{(by Prop.\ref{prop:12relations} $(\ref{AHH1})$ and $(\ref{AHH2})$)}

\displaystyle=z^{\pm}hX^{\pm}_{r+1}+q^{r-1-1/2}he^{\pm}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}\dot{x}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r}\notin RP_{r}.

So

\mathrm{Proj}^{\pm}_{G_{r}}(X^{\pm}_{r+1}g^{-1}_{i}T^{\pm}_{r+1})=0
for all
g_{i},
and hence

X^{\pm}_{r+1}\mapsto 0.

Let
y=T^{\pm}_{r+1}.

For any
h\in G_{r},
we have

\displaystyle T^{\pm}_{r+1}hT^{\pm}_{r+1}

\displaystyle=qe^{\pm}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{\pm}_{r}he^{\pm}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{\pm}_{r}\quad\text{(by Lemma \ref{Lem:T})}

\displaystyle=q{(^{s_{r+1}}h)}e^{\pm}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{\pm}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{\pm}_{r}

\displaystyle={{}^{{s}_{r+1}}h}T^{\pm}_{r+1}T^{\pm}_{r+1}

\displaystyle={{}^{s_{r+1}}h}(z^{\pm}T^{\pm}_{r+1}+e^{\pm}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r-1})\quad\text{(by Prop.\ref{prop:12relations} $(\ref{AHH1})$ and $(\ref{AHH2})$)}

\displaystyle=z^{\pm}e^{\pm}_{r}(^{s_{r+1}}h)T^{\pm}_{r+1}+(^{s_{r+1}}h)e^{\pm}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r-1}

\displaystyle=q^{\frac{1}{2}}z^{\pm}e^{\pm}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}he^{\pm}_{r}+(^{s_{r+1}}h)e^{\pm}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\quad\text{(by Lemma \ref{Lem:T})}.

Note that
q^{\frac{1}{2}}z^{\pm}e^{\pm}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}he^{\pm}_{r}\notin RP_{r},
hence

\mathrm{Proj}^{\pm}_{P_{r}}(T^{\pm}_{r+1}g^{-1}_{i}T^{\pm}_{r+1})=\begin{cases}(^{s_{r+1}}g_{i})^{-1}e^{\pm}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r-1}\,\,&\text{if}\,\,(^{s_{r+1}}g_{i})^{-1}\in P_{r};\\
0\,\,&\text{if}\,\,(^{s_{r+1}}g_{i})^{-1}\notin P_{r}.\end{cases}

However, by Lemma
2.5
(c),
G_{r}\cap{{}^{s_{r+1}}P_{r}}=P_{r-1}.
So if
(^{s_{r+1}}g_{i})^{-1}\in P_{r}
, we must have
g^{-1}_{i}\in P_{r-1}
and we can write

g^{-1}_{i}=v\times l\in P_{r-1}=U_{r-1}\rtimes G_{r-1}

where
l\in G_{r}
and
v\in U_{r-1}.

Since
v\in U_{r-1}
, by Lemma
2.5
(d), we have
{{}^{s_{r+1}}v}\in U_{r}.
It is easy to show that
{{}^{s_{r+1}}v}e^{+}_{r}=e^{+}_{r},

{{}^{s_{r+1}}v}e^{-}_{r}=\zeta(v)e^{-}_{r},

v^{-1}e^{+}_{r-1}=e^{+}_{r-1}
and
v^{-1}e^{-}_{r-1}=\zeta(v)e^{-}_{r-1}.

There is only one nonzero term since
g^{-1}_{i}\in P_{r-1}
and the nonzero term is exactly

\displaystyle\mathrm{Proj}^{\pm}_{P_{r}}((^{s_{r+1}}g_{i})^{-1}e^{\pm}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r-1})\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}g_{i}

\displaystyle=\mathrm{Proj}^{\pm}_{P_{r}}({{{}^{s_{r+1}}v}l}e^{\pm}_{r}e^{\pm}_{r-1})\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}l^{-1}v^{-1}

\displaystyle=e^{\pm}_{r-1}l\otimes l^{-1}e^{\pm}_{r-1}=e^{\pm}_{r-1}\otimes e^{\pm}_{r-1}.

(b)
We only prove for
\rm{LH}
. Note that
\rm{LH}
is the composition of the following bimodule maps:

\displaystyle e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r}\cong e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 1\otimes 1\otimes\eta^{-}_{L}}}{{\longrightarrow}}e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}\cdot e^{-}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{-}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 1\otimes H\otimes 1}}{{\longrightarrow}}e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}\cdot e^{+}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{-}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\varepsilon^{-}_{L}\otimes 1\otimes 1}}{{\longrightarrow}}RG_{r}\otimes_{RG_{r}}RG_{r}\cdot e^{+}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{-}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}\cong RG_{r}\cdot e^{+}_{r-1}\otimes_{RG_{r-1}}e^{-}_{r-1}\cdot RG_{r}.

By Proposition
2.7
, as an
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule, the bimodule
e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{+}_{r}
is generated by the unique element
H^{\prime}_{r+1}
, so we only need to compute the image of
H^{\prime}_{r+1}
. Similarly to
(a)
, we have

H^{\prime}_{r+1}\mapsto\sum\limits_{i=1}^{s}(\mathrm{Proj}^{+}_{P_{r}}(H^{\prime}_{r+1}g^{-1}_{i}H_{r+1})\otimes e^{-}_{r-1}g_{i})

For any
h\in G_{r},
we have

\displaystyle H^{\prime}_{r+1}hH_{r+1}

\displaystyle=qe^{-}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}he^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\quad\text{(by Lemma \ref{Lem:T})}

\displaystyle=q{(^{s_{r+1}}h)}e^{-}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{+}_{r}e^{+}_{r}\dot{s}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}

\displaystyle={{}^{{s}_{r+1}}h}H^{\prime}_{r+1}H_{r+1}

\displaystyle={{}^{s_{r+1}}h}e^{+}_{r}e^{-}_{r-1}\quad\text{(by Prop. \ref{prop:12relations} (\ref{Mixaff2}))}.

Hence

\mathrm{Proj}^{+}_{P_{r}}(H^{\prime}_{r+1}g^{-1}_{i}H_{r+1})=\begin{cases}(^{s_{r+1}}g_{i})^{-1}e^{+}_{r}e^{-}_{r-1}\,\,&\text{if}\,\,(^{s_{r+1}}g_{i})^{-1}\in P_{r};\\
0\,\,&\text{if}\,\,(^{s_{r+1}}g_{i})^{-1}\notin P_{r}.\end{cases}

Similarly to
(a)
, if
(^{s_{r+1}}g_{i})^{-1}\in P_{r}
, we must have
g^{-1}_{i}\in P_{r-1}
and we can write

g^{-1}_{i}=v\times l\in P_{r-1}=U_{r-1}\rtimes G_{r-1}

where
l\in G_{r}
and
v\in U_{r-1}.

Since
v\in U_{r-1}
, by Lemma
2.5
(d), we have
{{}^{s_{r+1}}v}\in U_{r}.
It is easy to show that
{{}^{s_{r+1}}v}e^{+}_{r}=e^{+}_{r}
and
v^{-1}e^{+}_{r-1}=e^{+}_{r-1}.

Hence there is only one nonzero term and the nonzero term is exactly

\displaystyle\mathrm{Proj}^{-}_{P_{r}}((^{s_{r+1}}g_{i})^{-1}e^{-}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1})\otimes e^{-}_{r-1}g_{i}

\displaystyle=\mathrm{Proj}^{-}_{P_{r}}({{{}^{s_{r+1}}v}l}e^{-}_{r}e^{+}_{r-1})\otimes e^{-}_{r-1}l^{-1}v^{-1}

\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\thicksim}le^{+}_{r-1}\otimes e^{-}_{r-1}l^{-1}=e^{+}_{r-1}\otimes e^{-}_{r-1}.

∎

Lemma 2.13
.

(a)

The natural transformation
\mathrm{LX}^{\pm}
is given by the
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule map

e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r}\to RG_{r},

e^{\pm}_{r}\mapsto 0,

X^{\pm}_{r+1}\,\mapsto\,-(t^{\pm})^{2},

T^{\pm}_{r+1}\mapsto 0.

(b)

The natural transformation
\mathrm{RX}^{\pm}
is given by
(RG_{r},RG_{r})
-bimodule map

RG_{r}\to e^{\pm}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{\pm}_{r},

1\mapsto-({t^{\pm}z^{\pm}})^{-1}X^{\pm}_{r+1}.

Proof.

We only prove
(a)
for
\rm{LX}^{-}
and
(b)
for
\rm{RX}^{-}
. The proof of others is similar.

(a)
Note that
\mathrm{LX}^{-}
is the composition of the following bimodule maps:

e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 1\otimes X^{-}}}{{\longrightarrow}}e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\varepsilon^{-}_{L}}}{{\longrightarrow}}RG_{r}.

The image of
e^{-}_{r}
is

e^{-}_{r}\mapsto X^{-}_{r+1}\mapsto\mathrm{Proj}^{-}_{P_{r}}(X^{-}_{r+1})=0.

The image of
X^{-}_{r+1}
is

X^{-}_{r+1}\mapsto(X^{-}_{r+1})^{2}\mapsto\mathrm{Proj}^{-}_{P_{r}}((X^{-}_{r+1})^{2}).

We have
(X^{-}_{r+1})^{2}=\beta^{2}q^{2r}e^{-}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}
and
e^{-}_{r}=\sum\limits_{g\in U_{r}}\zeta(g)g
. Then, by the proof of
[
13
, Prop.10.5.3]
, we have that
v_{1}\dot{x}_{r+1}v_{2}\dot{x}_{r+1}v_{3}\in P_{r}
if and only
v_{2}=1
where
v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\in V_{r}.
Hence,

\displaystyle(X^{-}_{r+1})^{2}

\displaystyle=\beta^{2}q^{2r}e^{-}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}

\displaystyle=\beta^{2}q^{2r}e^{-}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}e_{V_{r}}\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}

\displaystyle=\beta^{2}q^{2r}e^{-}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}\frac{1}{|V_{r}|}(1+\sum\limits_{v\in V_{r}-\{1\}}{v})\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}.

For any
v\in V_{r}-\{1\}
, we have
e^{-}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}v\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}\notin RP_{r}
and for
v=1
, we have
e^{-}_{r}\dot{x}_{r+1}v\dot{x}_{r+1}e^{-}_{r}=e^{-}_{r}(\dot{x}_{r+1})^{2}e^{-}_{r}.

Note that

(\dot{x}_{r+1})^{2}=\begin{cases}\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{G_{r+1}}&\text{if $G_{r}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2r+1}(q)$ or $\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2r}(q)$ };\\
\operatorname{diag}\nolimits(-1,\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{G_{r}},-1)&\text{if $G_{r}=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2r}(q)$},\end{cases}\,

so

e^{-}_{r}(\dot{x}_{r+1})^{2}e^{-}_{r}=\begin{cases}e^{-}_{r}&\text{if $G_{r}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2r+1}(q)$ or $\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2r}(q)$ };\\
\zeta(-1)e^{-}_{r}&\text{if $G_{r}=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2r}(q)$}.\end{cases}\,

Hence

X^{-}_{r+1}\mapsto\mathrm{Proj}^{-}_{P_{r}}((X^{-}_{r+1})^{2})=\mathrm{Proj}^{-}_{P_{r}}(\frac{\beta^{2}q^{2r}}{|V_{r}|}e^{-}_{r}(\dot{x}_{r+1})^{2}e^{-}_{r})\xrightarrow{\thicksim}-(t^{-})^{-2}.

The image of
T^{-}_{r+1}
is

T^{-}_{r+1}\mapsto T^{-}_{r+1}X^{-}_{r+1}\mapsto\mathrm{Proj}^{-}_{P_{r}}(T^{-}_{r+1}X^{-}_{r+1}).

By a similar argument as in the proof of Lemma
2.12
(b), we have the equality
\mathrm{Proj}^{-}_{P_{r}}(T^{-}_{r+1}X^{-}_{r+1})=0,
hence
T^{-}_{r+1}\mapsto 0.

(b)
Note that
\mathrm{RX}^{-}
is the composition of the following bimodule maps:

RG_{r}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eta^{-}_{R}}}{{\longrightarrow}}e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle 1\otimes X^{-}}}{{\longrightarrow}}e^{-}_{r}\cdot RG_{r+1}\cdot e^{-}_{r},

1\mapsto-({t^{-}z^{-}})^{-1}e^{-}_{r}\mapsto-({t^{-}z^{-}})^{-1}X^{-}_{r+1}.

∎

Now we can state the main proposition in this section.

.

(a)
