4.2.4.
Unique parametrization by colored weight functions

Based on the classification of irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal and Proposition
4.11
, we can determine a part of information of
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-)
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-)
, which can help us to give the unique parametrization of irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal.

For
G=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
case the parametrization for irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal
is completely determined.

For
G=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
, let
\rho=\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}},
then
\rho^{c}=\rho_{t_{+},-t_{-},\lambda_{\star}}
.
By Proposition
4.11
, we know that
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=(v-q^{t_{-}})(v+q^{-t_{-}})
or
(v-q^{-t_{-}})(v+q^{t_{-}})
.
On the other hand,

\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{-}(-v)(\rho^{c}).

So one of
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{c})
must be equal to
(v-q^{t_{-}})(v+q^{-t_{-}})
and then the other is equal to
(v-q^{-t_{-}})(v+q^{t_{-}}).

Hence we can relabel them such that
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}})=(v-q^{t_{-}})(v+q^{-t_{-}})
.

Similarly, for
G=\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
, we relabel them such that
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}})=(u-q^{t_{+}})(u+q^{-t_{+}})
and

\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}})=(v-q^{t_{-}})(v+q^{-t_{-}}).
Now we get
a unique parametrization for irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal,
see Table
3
.

Table 3.
Unique parametrization of irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal

\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2\bullet+1}(q)

\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2\bullet}(q)

\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2\bullet}(q)

\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\varepsilon}

\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}}

\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}}

t_{\pm}\in\mathbb{N},\varepsilon\in\{\pm 1\}

t_{+}\in\mathbb{N},t_{-}\in\mathbb{Z}

t_{\pm}\in\mathbb{Z}

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-):

-

-

(u-q^{t_{+}})(u+q^{-t_{+}})

\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-):

-

(v-q^{t_{-}})(v+q^{-t_{-}})

(v-q^{t_{-}})(v+q^{-t_{-}})

Remark 4.12
.

The colored weight functions in the three blanks of Table
3

will be determined in the next section, see Table
4
.

Proposition 4.13
.

Let
\rho,\rho^{\prime}
be both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal and
\rho^{\sharp}=\rho^{\prime\sharp}
.
Then
\rho=\rho^{\prime}
if and only if

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\prime})~~\text{ and }~~\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{\prime}).

Proof.

By Theorem
4.3
,

•

for
G=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
,
\rho^{\sharp}=\rho^{\prime\sharp}
if and only if
\rho^{\prime}\in\{\rho,\rho\cdot{\operatorname{det}}\}
;

•

for
G=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
,
\rho^{\sharp}=\rho^{\prime\sharp}
if and only if
\rho^{\prime}\in\{\rho,\rho^{c}\}
;

•

for
G=\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
,
\rho^{\sharp}=\rho^{\prime\sharp}
if and only if
\rho^{\prime}\in\{\rho,\rho^{c},\rho\cdot{\operatorname{det}},\rho^{c}\cdot{\operatorname{det}}\}
.

Note that
\rho
is both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal if and only if
\rho^{c}
(resp.
\rho\cdot{\operatorname{det}}
,
\rho^{c}\cdot{\operatorname{det}}
) is both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal.

On the other hand, by Proposition
4.11
,
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)({\operatorname{det}}\cdot\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{+}(-u)(\rho)
,
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)({\operatorname{det}}\cdot\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{-}(-v)(\rho),

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{c})=\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{c})=\mathbb{O}^{-}(-v)(\rho).

Then the lemma follows by the classification of modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal (see Lemma
4.5
) and Corollary
4.8
.
∎

4.3.
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
-categorification and complete invariants of
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits

By Theorem
4.10
, we know that the set
I_{+}
and
I_{-}

are both equal to
q^{\mathbb{Z}}\sqcup-q^{\mathbb{Z}}
. So in characteristic 0, we have
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}=\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{\infty}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{\infty}
,
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}=\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{\infty}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{\infty}
, and so
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
is isomorphic to four copies of Kac-Moody Lie algebra
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{\infty}.

Let
E^{+}=\bigoplus_{i\in I_{+}}E^{+}_{i}
and
F^{+}=\bigoplus_{i\in I_{+}}F^{+}_{i}
(resp.
E^{-}=\bigoplus_{i^{\prime}\in I_{-}}E^{-}_{i^{\prime}}
and
F^{-}=\bigoplus_{i^{\prime}\in I_{-}}F^{-}_{i^{\prime}}
) be the decomposition of the functors into generalized

i
-eigenspaces for
X^{+}
(resp. generalized

i^{\prime}
-eigenspaces for
X^{-}
) on
E^{+}
and
F^{+}
(resp.
E^{-}
and
F^{-}
). Then

\{[E^{+}_{i}],[F^{+}_{i}],[E^{-}_{i^{\prime}}],[F^{-}_{i^{\prime}}]\}_{i\in I_{+},i^{\prime}\in I_{-}}

act as the Chevalley generators
\{e^{+}_{i},f^{+}_{i},e^{-}_{i^{\prime}},f^{-}_{i^{\prime}}\}_{i\in I_{+},i^{\prime}\in I_{-}}
of
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
on
the Grothendieck group
[KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]
of
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
and many problems on
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
have a Lie-theoretic
counterpart:

•

irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal correspond to highest weight vectors of
\mathfrak{g}
-module
[KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]
;

•

the decomposition of
[KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]
as
\mathfrak{g}
-module into
a direct sum of irreducible highest weight
modules are parametrized by irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal;

•

the colored weight functions
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\sigma),

\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\sigma)
and the weight
{\operatorname{wt}}(\sigma)
for any irreducible
\sigma\in KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
are determined mutually.

So once we can determine
{\operatorname{wt}}(\rho)
the weight of irreducible modules
\rho
which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal, we can compute the weights of all irreducible modules.
In this section, we will show that the colored weight functions
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)
,
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)
and uniform projection can distinguish all irreducible modules of
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
. This extends Proposition
4.13
which only concerns the case where the modules are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal.

4.3.1.
Residues and contents

We fix
\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{l})\in{I}^{l}
, and assume that
{I}
is stable under the multiplication by

q
and
q^{-1}
.
Let
A\in Y(\boldsymbol{\lambda})
be the box which lies in
the
i
-th row and
j
-th column of the diagram of

\lambda^{p}
.
The
(\boldsymbol{\xi},q)
-shifted residue
of the node
A
is the element of
{I}
given by

q\text{-}\!\operatorname{res}\nolimits^{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(A)=q^{j-i}\xi_{p}.
If
\boldsymbol{\lambda}
,
\boldsymbol{\mu}
are
l
-partitions such
that
|\boldsymbol{\mu}|=|\boldsymbol{\lambda}|+1
we write
q\text{-}\!\operatorname{res}\nolimits^{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\lambda})=i
if
Y(\boldsymbol{\mu})
is obtained by
adding a node of
(\boldsymbol{\xi},q)
-shifted residue
i
to
Y(\boldsymbol{\lambda})
. We call the node a removable
i
-node of
\boldsymbol{\mu}
and an addable node of
\boldsymbol{\lambda}
.
A
charge
of the tuple
\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{l})
is an
l
-tuple of integers

\boldsymbol{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{l})
such that
\xi_{p}=q^{s_{p}}
for all
p=1,\ldots,l
.
Conversely, given
{I}\subset R^{\times}
and
q\in R^{\times}
, any

l
-tuple of integers
\boldsymbol{s}\in\mathbb{Z}^{l}
defines a tuple
\boldsymbol{\xi}=(q^{s_{1}},\ldots,q^{s_{l}})
with
charge
\boldsymbol{s}
.
The
\boldsymbol{s}
-shifted content

of the box
A=(i,j,p)
is the integer
\text{cont}^{\boldsymbol{s}}(A)=s_{p}+j-i
. Similarly, if
\boldsymbol{\lambda}
,
\boldsymbol{\mu}
are
l
-partitions such
that
|\boldsymbol{\mu}|=|\boldsymbol{\lambda}|+1
we write
\text{cont}^{\boldsymbol{s}}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\lambda})=i
if
Y(\boldsymbol{\mu})
is obtained by
adding a node of
\boldsymbol{s}
-shifted content
i
to
Y(\lambda)
.
It is related to the residue of
A
by the formula
q\text{-}\!\operatorname{res}\nolimits^{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(A)=q^{\text{cont}^{\boldsymbol{s}}(A)}
.

4.3.2.
Fock spaces

Recall that a
Fock space

\mathbf{F}(\boldsymbol{\xi})

is the
\mathbb{C}
-vector
space with basis

\{|\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle_{I}\,|\,\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{l}\}
and the action of
e_{i},f_{i}
for all
i\in{I}
given by

f_{i}(|\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle_{{I}})=\sum\limits_{q\text{-}\!\operatorname{res}\nolimits^{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\lambda})=i}|\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle_{{I}},

e_{i}(|\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle_{{I}})=\sum\limits_{q\text{-}\!\operatorname{res}\nolimits^{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\lambda})=i}|\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle_{{I}}.

For brevity, we will omit the subscript
{I}
if there is no confusion. The basis

\{|\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle\,|\,\boldsymbol{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{l}\}
is
called the

standard monomial basis
, where every element is a weight vector.

Now we describe the action of
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{{I}}
on
\mathbf{F}(\boldsymbol{\xi})
in the case where
q
has infinite
order, i.e.,
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{{I}}
is isomorphic to a direct sum of
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}_{\infty}
.
For an
l
-partition
\boldsymbol{\lambda}
and
i\in{I}
we define

\displaystyle N_{i}(\boldsymbol{\lambda}|\boldsymbol{\xi})=\sharp\{\text{ addable $i$-nodes of $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$}\}-\sharp\{\text{ removable $i$-nodes of $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$}\}.

Let
\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{l})\in I^{l}
.
Now we can state the following theorem.

Theorem 4.14

(
[
58
]
)
.

The following formulas define on
\mathbf{F}(\boldsymbol{\xi})
the structure of an integrable
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{{I}}
-module:

\displaystyle f_{i}|\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle=\sum_{q\text{-}\!\operatorname{res}\nolimits^{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\lambda})=i}|\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle,

\displaystyle e_{i}|\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle=\sum_{q\text{-}\!\operatorname{res}\nolimits^{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\lambda})=i}|\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle,

\displaystyle\alpha^{\vee}_{i}|\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle={N_{i}(\boldsymbol{\lambda}|\boldsymbol{\xi})}|\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle.

For this action the weight of a standard basis element is

(4.23)

\mathrm{wt}(|\boldsymbol{\lambda},\boldsymbol{\xi}\rangle)=\sum_{i\in I}N_{i}(\boldsymbol{\lambda}|\boldsymbol{\xi})\Lambda_{i}.

4.3.3.
Content function and
(q,\pm)
-residue function

Let
|\lambda,s\rangle\in\mathscr{P}\times\mathbb{Z}
be a charged partition,
then we define its content function by

(4.24)

\displaystyle\mathbb{O}_{|\lambda,s\rangle}(u)=\frac{\prod\limits_{\text{$b$ addable }}(u-\text{cont}^{s}(b))}{\prod\limits_{\text{$b$ removable }}(u-\text{cont}^{s}(b))}

and
(q,\epsilon)
-residue function by

(4.25)

\displaystyle\mathbb{O}^{(q,\epsilon)}_{|\lambda,s\rangle}(u)=\frac{\prod\limits_{\text{$b$ addable }}(u-\epsilon\cdot q^{\text{cont}^{s}(b)})}{\prod\limits_{\text{$b$ removable }}(u-\epsilon\cdot q^{\text{cont}^{s}(b)})}

where
b
runs over the boxes of the Young diagram
Y(\lambda)
of
\lambda
and
\epsilon\in\{\pm\}.

Example 4.15
.

Let
\lambda=(4,1,1)
and
s=1.

The Young diagram of
\lambda
with its
s
-shifted contents is

\begin{array}[]{|c|c|c|c|}\hline\cr 1&2&3&4\\
\hline\cr 0\\
\cline{1-1}\cr-1\\
\cline{1-1}\cr\end{array}.

Then we have
\mathbb{O}_{|\lambda,s\rangle}(u)=\frac{(u-5)(u-1)(u+2)}{(u-4)(u+1)},

\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\lambda,s\rangle}(u)=\frac{(u-q^{5})(u-q)(u-q^{-2})}{(u-q^{4})(u-q^{-1})}
and
\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\lambda,s\rangle}(u)=\frac{(u+q^{5})(u+q)(u+q^{-2})}{(u+q^{4})(u+q^{-1})}.

4.3.4.
Interlacing integer sequences and charged partitions

Definition 4.16

(
[
36
]
)
.

Two integer sets (or increasing integer sequences)
y_{1},\,\ldots,y_{n-1}\in\mathbb{Z}
and

x_{1},\,\ldots,x_{n-1},x_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}
are said to be
interlacing
, if and only if

x_{1}<y_{1}<x_{2}<\ldots<x_{n-1}<y_{n-1}<x_{n}.

The number
c=\sum x_{k}-\sum y_{k}
is called the
center
of
interlacing integer sequences.

An interlacing integer sequences is identified with a function
\omega
on
\mathbb{R}
such that

(1)

\omega
is piecewise linear with slopes being either
1
or
-1
,

(2)

local maxima and minima are located on
\mathbb{Z}
,

(3)

\omega(x)=x-c
when
x\gg 0
and
\omega(x)=c-x
when
x\ll 0
for some
c\in\mathbb{Z}
.

The sequence can be recovered from its local minima
x_{1}<x_{2}<\cdots<x_{n}

and local maxima
y_{1}<y_{2}<\cdots<y_{n-1}
. Note that the center is
c.

Each charged partition
|\mu,c\rangle\in\mathscr{P}\times\mathbb{Z}
uniquely defines two interlacing integer sequences as follows:

•

x_{1}<x_{2}<\cdots<x_{n}
is the ordered list of all
c
-shifted content
\text{cont}^{c}(b)
of addable box
b
with respect to the Young diagram of
\mu
,

•

y_{1}<y_{2}<\cdots<y_{n-1}
is the ordered list of all
c
-shifted content
\text{cont}^{c}(b)
of removeable box
b
with respect to the Young diagram of
\mu
.

Conversely, the region

S_{\omega}=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:|u-c|\leq v\leq\omega(u)\}

between the graphs of functions
v=\omega(u)
and
v=|u-c|
corresponds to the shape of a
Young diagram, which determines a partition
\mu
(see Example
4.18
). Together with the center
c=\sum x_{k}-\sum y_{k}
, we finally get the charged partition
|\mu,c\rangle
.

Lemma 4.17

(
[
36
]
)
.

The above two maps are inverse to each other, so they give a bijection between the space of interlacing integer sequences and charged partitions
\mathscr{P}\times\mathbb{Z}.

Example 4.18
.

Let
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}x_{1}}<{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}x_{2}}<{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}x_{3}}<{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}x_{4}}

and
\color[rgb]{0,1,0}{y_{1}}<\color[rgb]{0,1,0}{y_{2}}<\color[rgb]{0,1,0}{y_{3}}
be
the interlacing integer sequences

{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{-4}}<{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{-2}}<{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{0}}<{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{3}}\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}{-3}}<{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}{-1}}<{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}{2}}.

The corresponding function
\omega
is represented graphically by the boldened trajectory in the following diagram.
Note that center of this interlacing integer sequences is
c=-1

and we can get the partition
\mu=(4,2,1)
. Finally, we get the charged partition
|\mu,c\rangle.

x_{4}
y_{3}
x_{3}
y_{2}
x_{2}
y_{1}

Given a charged partition
|\mu,c\rangle\in\mathscr{P}\times\mathbb{Z}
, let
x_{1}<x_{2}<\cdots<x_{n}

and
y_{1}<y_{2}<\cdots<y_{n-1}
be the corresponding interlacing integer sequences then by the definition of content function, we have

\mathbb{O}_{|\mu,c\rangle}(u)=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(u-x_{i})}{\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(u-y_{j})}.

Corollary 4.19
.

(a)

The content function
\mathbb{O}_{\bullet}(u):\mathscr{P}\times\mathbb{Z}\to K(u)
is an injective map.

(b)

Let
\epsilon\in\{\pm\}.

The
(q,\epsilon)
-residue function
\mathbb{O}^{(q,\epsilon)}_{\bullet}(u):\mathscr{P}\times\mathbb{Z}\to K(u)
is also an injective map.

Proof.

(a)
Note that the content functions for charged partitions and interlacing sequences determines each other. The corollary is deduced from Lemma
4.17
.

(b)
Note that the content function
\mathbb{O}_{\bullet}(u)
are 1-1 correspondent to
(q,\epsilon)
-residue function
\mathbb{O}^{(q,\epsilon)}_{\bullet}(u)
since
q\in\mathbb{R}_{>1}
.
∎

Remark 4.20
.

It is straightforward to verify that
\mathbb{O}_{|\mu,c\rangle}(u)
(resp.
\mathbb{O}^{(q,\epsilon)}_{|\mu,c\rangle}(u)
) is a polynomial (i.e., an element of
K[u]
rather than merely
K(u)
) if and only if
\mu=\emptyset.
Indeed, if
\mu\neq\emptyset,
then the removable boxes of the Young diagram
Y(\mu)
is non-empty. Since all addable and removable boxes possess distinct contents, it follows that
\mathbb{O}_{|\mu,c\rangle}(u)
(resp.
\mathbb{O}^{(q,\epsilon)}_{|\mu,c\rangle}(u)
) can not be a polynomial in this case.

4.3.5.
Complete invariants of
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits

The main task of this subsection is to show that the colored weight functions
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)
,
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)
and uniform projection can distinguish all irreducible modules of
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
.

For short, we will write
\rho_{t_{+}\,t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)}=\rho_{t_{+}\,t_{-},\lambda_{\star}}
if
G=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
or
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
and
\rho_{t_{+}\,t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)}=\rho_{t_{+}\,t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon}
if
G=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q).

We know that the irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal have the form
\rho_{t_{+}\,t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)}
.
Now let
(KG_{\bullet},\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)})\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
be the Serre subcategory of
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
generated by the Kac-Moody 2-category
\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}})
acting on
\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)}
. Since the category
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
is semisimple,
it can actually be generated by
the modules
(F^{-})^{m_{-}}(F^{+})^{m_{+}}(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)})
for all
m_{+},m_{-}\in\mathbb{N}
. Then we have that

[KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]=\bigoplus_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)}[(KG_{\bullet},\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)})\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]

is the decomposition of
[KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]
as
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
-module into
a direct sum of irreducible highest weight
modules, and the image of
\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)}
in
[KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]
is a highest weight vector. In particular, the highest weight of
[\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)}]
is determined by
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)})
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)})
.

We have the following theorem.

Theorem 4.21
.

Let
\rho=\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)}
be both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal. We assume that
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=(u-q^{s_{1}^{+}})(u+q^{s_{2}^{+}})
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=(v-q^{s_{1}^{-}})(v+q^{s_{2}^{-}}).

\mathrm{(a)}

The operators
[F^{+}_{i}],[E^{+}_{i}],[F^{-}_{i^{\prime}}],[E^{-}_{i^{\prime}}]
for
i\in{I}_{+}
,
i^{\prime}\in{I}_{-}
yield a representation of

\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
on
[(KG_{\bullet},\rho)\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]
.

\mathrm{(b)}

We write
\Upsilon(\Lambda_{+})=(\mu^{+}_{1},\mu^{+}_{2})

and
\Upsilon(\Lambda_{-})=(\mu^{-}_{1},\mu^{-}_{2}).

Then the map

|(\mu^{+}_{1},\mu^{+}_{2}),(q^{s_{1}^{+}},-q^{s^{+}_{2}})\rangle\otimes|(\mu^{-}_{1},\mu^{-}_{2}),(q^{s^{-}_{1}},-q^{s^{-}_{2}})\rangle\otimes\mapsto[\rho_{\Lambda_{+},\Lambda_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon^{\prime})}]

gives an

\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
-module isomorphism

\mathbf{F}(q^{s^{+}_{1}},-q^{s^{+}_{2}})\otimes\mathbf{F}(q^{s^{-}_{1}},-q^{s^{-}_{2}})\overset{\sim}{\to}[(KG_{\bullet},\rho)\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits],

where
\epsilon^{\prime}=(-1)^{\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda_{-})}\epsilon
for
G_{n}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
case and for other cases
\epsilon^{\prime}=\emptyset
.

\mathrm{(c)}

For
G_{n}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
case let
\epsilon^{\prime}=(-1)^{\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda_{-})}\epsilon
and for other cases let
\epsilon^{\prime}=\emptyset.
We have

(c1)

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho_{\Lambda_{+},\Lambda_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon^{\prime})})=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\mu_{1}^{+},s_{1}^{+}\rangle}(u)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\mu_{2}^{+},s_{2}^{+}\rangle}(u)
,

(c2)

\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho_{\Lambda_{+},\Lambda_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon^{\prime})})=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\mu_{1}^{-},s_{1}^{-}\rangle}(v)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\mu_{2}^{-},s^{-}_{2}\rangle}(v).

Proof.

The proofs of
(a)
and
(b)
are similar to
[
39
, Theorem 5.23]
, see also
[
19
, Proposition 6.9]
. In particular, for the
G=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
case, the sign
\epsilon^{\prime}\in\{\pm 1\}
is because of (
4.21
) and
(\ref{O2n+1(2)}).

For
(c)
, note that under this isomorphism, we can compute the weight of any irreducible modules, hence colored weight functions
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-)
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-)
by (
4.23
) and (
1.29
).
∎

Now we can prove Theorem C in the Introduction, and we restate it as follows.

Theorem 4.22
.

Let
G_{n}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q),\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
or
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{\pm}(q)
and
\rho,\rho^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G_{n}).

(a)

We have
\rho=\rho^{\prime}
if and only if the following hold:

(1)

\rho^{\sharp}=\rho^{\prime\sharp},

(2)

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\prime})
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{\prime}).

(b)

If
\rho
and
\rho^{\prime}
are quadratic unipotent, then
\rho=\rho^{\prime}
if and only if

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\prime})
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{\prime}).

(c)

If
\rho
and
\rho^{\prime}
are unipotent, then
\rho=\rho^{\prime}
if and only if

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\prime}).

Proof.

(a)

We assume that
\rho=\rho_{\Lambda_{+},\Lambda_{-},\lambda_{\star}}\in(KG_{\bullet},\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}})\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
(or
\rho=\rho_{\Lambda_{+},\Lambda_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon^{\prime}}\in(KG_{\bullet},\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon})\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
).
Then by Theorem
4.21
, we know that

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\mu_{1}^{+},s_{1}^{+}\rangle}(u)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\mu_{2}^{+},s_{2}^{+}\rangle}(u)~\text{and}~\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\mu_{1}^{-},s_{1}^{-}\rangle}(v)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\mu_{2}^{-},s^{-}_{2}\rangle}(v).

By Theorem
4.3
, we have

•

for
G=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
,
\rho^{\sharp}=\rho^{\prime\sharp}
if and only if
\rho^{\prime}\in\{\rho,\rho\cdot{\operatorname{det}}\}
;

•

for
G=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
,
\rho^{\sharp}=\rho^{\prime\sharp}
if and only if
\rho^{\prime}\in\{\rho,\rho^{c}\}
;

•

for
G=\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n}(q)
,
\rho^{\sharp}=\rho^{\prime\sharp}
if and only if
\rho^{\prime}\in\{\rho,\rho^{c},\rho\cdot{\operatorname{det}},\rho^{c}\cdot{\operatorname{det}}\}
.

We only prove the case
G=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q),
and the proofs of other cases are similar.
For
G=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n},
we have
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{c})=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\mu_{1}^{+},s_{1}^{+}\rangle}(u)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\mu_{2}^{+},s_{2}^{+}\rangle}(u)
and

\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{c})=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\mu_{1}^{-},s_{1}^{-}\rangle}(-v)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\mu_{2}^{-},s^{-}_{2}\rangle}(-v)=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\mu_{2}^{-},s^{-}_{2}\rangle}(v)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\mu_{1}^{-},s_{1}^{-}\rangle}(v).

By Proposition
4.19
, we know that
\mathbb{O}^{(q,\epsilon)}_{\bullet}(v)
is injective from
\mathscr{P}\times\mathbb{Z}
to
K(v)
for
\epsilon\in\{\pm\}
. Note that the poles and zeros of
\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\mu,s\rangle}(v)
belong to
q^{\mathbb{Z}}
and the poles and zeros of
\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\mu,s\rangle}(v)
belong to
-q^{\mathbb{Z}}
. Hence
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{c})=\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)
if and only if
|\mu_{1}^{-},s_{1}^{-}\rangle=|\mu_{2}^{-},s^{-}_{2}\rangle
, i.e.,
\Lambda_{-}=\Lambda^{t}_{-},

which is equivalent to

\rho=\rho^{c}.

(b)

Assume that
\rho
and
\rho^{\prime}
are quadratic unipotent, then
\rho=\rho_{\Lambda_{+},\Lambda_{-},(\epsilon)}
and
\rho^{\prime}=\rho_{\Lambda^{\prime}_{+},\Lambda^{\prime}_{-},(\epsilon^{\prime})}.

We have

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\mu_{1}^{+},s_{1}^{+}\rangle}(u)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\mu_{2}^{+},s_{2}^{+}\rangle}(u)~\text{and}~\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|\mu_{1}^{-},s_{1}^{-}\rangle}(v)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|\mu_{2}^{-},s^{-}_{2}\rangle}(v).

Similarly, we have

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\prime})=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|{\mu^{\prime}}_{1}^{+},{s^{\prime}}_{1}^{+}\rangle}(u)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|{\mu^{\prime}}_{2}^{+},{s^{\prime}}_{2}^{+}\rangle}(u)~\text{and}~\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{\prime})=\mathbb{O}^{(q,+)}_{|{\mu^{\prime}}_{1}^{-},{s^{\prime}}_{1}^{-}\rangle}(v)\cdot\mathbb{O}^{(q,-)}_{|{\mu^{\prime}}_{2}^{-},{s^{\prime}}^{-}_{2}\rangle}(v).

Then the conditions
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\prime})
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho^{\prime})
imply

\mathbb{O}^{(q,\pm)}_{|\mu_{i}^{+},s_{i}^{+}\rangle}(u)=\mathbb{O}^{(q,\pm)}_{|{\mu^{\prime}}_{i}^{+},{s^{\prime}}_{i}^{+}\rangle}(u)~\text{and}~\mathbb{O}^{(q,\pm)}_{|\mu_{i}^{-},s_{i}^{-}\rangle}(v)=\mathbb{O}^{(q,\pm)}_{|{\mu^{\prime}}_{i}^{-},{s^{\prime}}_{i}^{-}\rangle}(v)

for
i=1,2
.
By the injectivity of
\mathbb{O}^{(q,\epsilon)}_{\bullet}(u)
, we must have

|\mu_{i}^{+},s_{i}^{+}\rangle=|{\mu^{\prime}}_{i}^{+},{s^{\prime}}_{i}^{+}\rangle~\text{and}~|\mu_{i}^{-},s_{i}^{-}\rangle=|{\mu^{\prime}}_{i}^{-},{s^{\prime}}_{i}^{-}\rangle

for
i=1,2
,
which imply that
\Lambda_{+}=\Lambda^{\prime}_{+}
and
\Lambda_{-}=\Lambda^{\prime}_{-}
(also
\epsilon=\epsilon^{\prime}
for
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
case). So
(b)
follows.

The proof of
(c)
is similar to
(b).

∎

By Lemma
4.5
and Remark
4.20
, we have the following corollary, which provides a characterization of
F^{\pm}
-cuspidal modules.

Corollary 4.23
.

Let
\rho\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G).

Then

(a)

\rho
is
F^{+}
-cuspidal if and only if
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)
is a polynomial;

(b)

\rho
is
F^{-}
-cuspidal if and only if
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)
is a polynomial.

In particular, for a unipotent irreducible module
\rho
, it is cuspidal if and only if
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)
is a polynomial.

5.
Theta correspondence and decategorification

In this section, we will use the theta correspondence to
determine all colored weight functions for irreducible modules which are both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal.
This gives a complete answer to the action of the Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
on the Grothendieck group
[KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]
.

5.1.
Theta correspondence

In this section, we will recall some basic results for the theta correspondence.

5.1.1.
Definition

Let
V
be a vector space over
\mathbb{F}_{q}
equipped with a non-degenerate quadratic from
\langle\,\,,\,\,\rangle_{V}:V\times V\to\mathbb{F}_{q}
and let
G(V)
be the isometry group of
\langle\,\,,\,\,\rangle_{V}.

V
has a Witt decomposition

V=V_{a}\oplus X\oplus Y

where
V_{a}
is anisotropic and its orthogonal complement
V_{a}^{\perp}=X\oplus Y

consists of isotropic subspaces
X
and
Y
. to organize such spaces into Witt towers, defined as

\mathcal{V}:=\{V_{a},V_{a}\oplus\mathbb{H},V_{a}\oplus\mathbb{H}^{\oplus 2},\cdots\}

a collection of spaces formed by successively adjoining copies of the hyperbolic plane
\mathbb{H}
to a fixed anisotropic space
V_{a}
. Clearly,
V
itself is an element of
\mathcal{V}
. Now, let
(V,V^{\prime})
be a dual pair. We consider the following types of related Witt towers:

(
I
)

V
is an orthogonal space, and
\mathcal{V}^{\prime}
is the Witt towers of symplectic spaces containing
V^{\prime}
;

(
II
)

V
is a symplectic space, and
\mathcal{V}^{\prime+}
(resp.
\mathcal{V}^{\prime-}
) is the Witt towers of even-dimensional orthogonal spaces with trivial (resp. two-dimensional) anisotropic kernel which contains
V^{\prime}
;

(
III
)

V
is a symplectic space, and
\mathcal{V}^{\prime}
is the Witt towers of odd-dimensional orthogonal spaces containing
V^{\prime}
.

We fix a non-trivial character
\psi:(\mathbb{F}_{q},+)\to\mathbb{C}^{\times}
.
Let
\omega_{G,G^{\prime}}=\omega_{G,G^{\prime}}^{\psi}
be the Weil representation of
G(V\otimes V^{\prime})
constructed in
[
28
]
.
It has a non-negative integral decomposition

\omega_{G,G^{\prime}}=\sum_{\rho\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G),\rho^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G^{\prime})}m_{\rho,\rho^{\prime}}\rho\otimes\rho^{\prime}

where
{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G)
denotes the set of irreducible characters of
G
.
We say that
(\rho,\rho^{\prime})

occurs
in the
theta correspondence
(or
Howe correspondence
) if
m_{\rho,\rho^{\prime}}\neq 0
,
i.e., there is a relation

\displaystyle\Theta_{G,G^{\prime}}=\{\,(\rho,\rho^{\prime})\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G)\times{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G^{\prime})\mid m_{\rho,\rho^{\prime}}\neq 0\,\}

between
{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G)
and
{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G^{\prime})
.

5.1.2.
First occurrence

Let
G_{n}
(or
G^{\prime}_{n}
) be one of
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q),\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n}^{\pm}(q)
. Assume that
(G_{n},G^{\prime}_{n^{\prime}})
is a dual pair and
\sigma\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G_{n})
and
\sigma^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G^{\prime}_{n^{\prime}})
. Define

\Theta_{G^{\prime}_{n^{\prime}}(\sigma)}=\{\sigma^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G^{\prime}_{n^{\prime}})|(\sigma,\sigma^{\prime})\,\,\text{occurs in }\Theta_{G_{n},G^{\prime}_{n^{\prime}}}\}

and

\Theta_{G_{n}(\sigma^{\prime})}=\{\sigma\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G_{n})|(\sigma,\sigma^{\prime})\,\,\text{occurs in }\Theta_{G_{n},G^{\prime}_{n^{\prime}}}\}.

It is known that
\Theta_{G^{\prime}_{n^{\prime}}(\sigma)}\neq\emptyset
implies
\Theta_{G^{\prime}_{n^{\prime\prime}}(\sigma)}\neq\emptyset
for all
n^{\prime\prime}>n^{\prime}.

We say that
(\sigma,\sigma^{\prime})
occurring in
\Theta_{G_{n},G^{\prime}_{n^{\prime}}}
is a
first occurrence
if
\Theta_{G^{\prime}_{n^{\prime}-1}}(\sigma)=\emptyset
and
\Theta_{G_{n-1}}(\sigma^{\prime})=\emptyset.

If
(G,G^{\prime})=(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q),\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon}_{2n}(q))
,
then the unipotent characters are preserved by
\Theta_{G,G^{\prime}}
(
[
2
]
theorem 3.5),
i.e., we can write

\displaystyle\omega_{G,G^{\prime},1}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal{E}(G,1),\ \rho^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}(G^{\prime},1)}m_{\rho,\rho^{\prime}}\rho\otimes\rho^{\prime},

\displaystyle\Theta_{G,G^{\prime},1}

\displaystyle=\Theta_{G,G^{\prime}}\cap(\mathcal{E}(G,1)\times\mathcal{E}(G^{\prime},1))

where
\omega_{G,G^{\prime},1}
denotes the unipotent part of
\omega_{G,G^{\prime}}
.
For the theta correspondence on unipotent characters,
the following theorem is well-known, due to Adams and Moy.

Theorem 5.1

(
[
1
]
)
.

Let
\rho^{\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits}_{t}
be the unique unipotent cuspidal module of
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2t(t+1)}(q)
as defined in §
4.1.3
and
\pi_{t}^{\alpha}
and
\pi_{t}^{\beta}
(following the notation of
[
1
]
) are the unipotent cuspidal modules of
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t}}_{2t^{2}}(q)
, where
\epsilon_{t}=(-1)^{t}.
Then we have the following:

(a)

(\pi_{t}^{\alpha},\rho_{t}^{\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits})
first occurs in the correspondence for the pair
(\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t}}_{2t^{2}}(q),\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2t(t+1)}(q))

and

(b)

(\pi_{t}^{\beta},\rho^{\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits}_{t-1})
first occurs in the correspondence for the pair
(\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t}}_{2t^{2}}(q),\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2t(t-1)}(q)).

Remark 5.2
.

Recall that in §
4.1.3
, we label the two unipotent cuspidal modules of
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t}}_{2t^{2}}(q)
by
\rho_{t}^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}
and
\rho_{-t}^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}
. In Theorem
5.9
(2), we will examine this parametrization in relation to the one introduced by Adams and Moy.

5.1.3.
Modified Lusztig’s Jordan decomposition

Let
G
be one of
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q),

\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
and
\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon}_{2n}(q).
For
s\in G^{*},
in §
4.1.6
, we define
G^{(+)}
,
G^{(-)}
and
G^{(\star)}
such that
C_{G^{*}}(s)\simeq G^{(+)}\times G^{(-)}\times G^{(\star)}
.
We now define

(5.1)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\underline{G}^{(+)}&=\begin{cases}G^{(+)},\,&\text{ if $G$ is an orthogonal group;}\\
(G^{(+)})^{*},\,&\text{ if $G$ is a symplectic group.}\end{cases}\end{split}

Then

(5.2)

(\underline{G}^{(+)},G^{(-)})=\begin{cases}(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n^{(+)}}(q),\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n^{(-)}}(q)),&\text{if $G=\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)$};\\
(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n^{(+)}}(q),\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon^{(-)}}_{2n^{(-)}}(q)),&\text{if $G=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)$};\\
(\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon^{(+)}}_{2n^{(+)}}(q),\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon^{(-)}}_{2n^{(-)}}(q)),&\text{if $G=\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon}_{2n}(q)$}\end{cases}

for some non-negative integers
n^{(+)},n^{(-)}
depending on
s
,
and some
\epsilon^{(+)},\epsilon^{(-)}\in\{\pm 1\}
(see §
4.1.6
(
4.13
)).

Then a
modified Lusztig’s Jordan decomposition
defined in
[
52
,
53
]

(5.3)

\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s}\colon\mathcal{E}(G,s)\rightarrow\mathcal{E}(\underline{G}^{(+)}\times G^{(-)}\times G^{(\star)},1)

can be written as

(5.4)

\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s}(\rho)=\rho^{(+)}\otimes\rho^{(-)}\otimes\rho^{(\star)}

where
\rho^{({\dagger})}\in\mathcal{E}(G^{({\dagger})},1)
for
{\dagger}\in\{-,\star\}
or
\mathcal{E}(\underline{G}^{({\dagger})},1)
for
{\dagger}=+
.

Similar to Lusztig correspondence, combining
\mathcal{L}_{1}
for
\underline{G}^{(+)}\times G^{(-)}\times G^{(\star)}

and the inverse of
\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s}
in (
5.3
):

\mathcal{S}_{\underline{G}^{(+)}}\times\mathcal{S}_{G^{(-)}}\times\mathcal{S}_{G^{(*)}}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}(\underline{G}^{(+)}\times G^{(-)}\times G^{(\star)},1)\rightarrow\mathcal{E}(G,s^{(+)}\times s^{(-)}\times s^{(\star)})

we obtain a bijection

(5.5)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\underline{\mathcal{L}}_{s}\colon\mathcal{S}_{\underline{G}^{(+)}}\times\mathcal{S}_{G^{(-)}}\times\mathcal{S}_{G^{(\star)}}&\rightarrow\mathcal{E}(G,s)\\
(\Lambda_{+},\Lambda_{-},\lambda_{\star})&\mapsto\rho_{\Lambda_{+},\Lambda_{-},\lambda_{\star}}.\end{split}

Such a bijection
\underline{\mathcal{L}}_{s}
is called a
modified Lusztig parametrization
. Since
\mathcal{E}(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q),1)
and
\mathcal{E}(\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q),1)
are parametrized by the same Lusztig symbols
\mathcal{S}_{\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}}=\mathcal{S}_{\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}}
via a unique way (see
[
53
, Proposition 4.9]
), the modified Lusztig parametrization coincides with Lusztig parametrization defined in §
4.1.7
.

5.1.4.
Pan’s results

Pan in
[
52
]
proved the commutativity (up to a twist of the sign
character) between modified Lusztig’s Jordan decomposition and theta correspondence.

For the symplectic-even orthogonal dual pairs, we have the following proposition.

Proposition 5.3

(
[
52
]
)
.

Let
(G,G^{\prime})=(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q),\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon}_{2n^{\prime}}(q))
,
and let
\rho\in\mathcal{E}(G,s)
and
\rho^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}(G^{\prime},s^{\prime})
for some semisimple elements
s\in G^{*}

and
s^{\prime}\in(G^{\prime*})^{0}
.
Let
\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s},\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s^{\prime}}
be any modified Lusztig’s Jordan decomposition.
Write
\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s}(\rho)=\rho^{(+)}\otimes\rho^{(-)}\otimes\rho^{(\star)}
and

\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s^{\prime}}(\rho^{\prime})=\rho^{\prime(+)}\otimes\rho^{\prime(-)}\otimes\rho^{\prime(\star)}
.
Then
(\rho,\rho^{\prime})
occurs in
\Theta_{G,G^{\prime}}
if and only if the following conditions hold:

•

s^{(\star)}=s^{\prime(\star)}
(up to conjugation), and
\rho^{(\star)}=\rho^{\prime(\star)}
;

•

G^{(-)}\simeq G^{\prime(-)}
, and
\rho^{(-)}=\rho^{\prime(-)}
or
\rho^{(-)}=\rho^{\prime(-)}\cdot{\operatorname{det}}
;

•

(\rho^{(+)},\rho^{\prime(+)})
or
(\rho^{(+)},\rho^{\prime(+)}\cdot{\operatorname{det}})
occurs in
\Theta_{\underline{G}^{(+)},\underline{G}^{\prime(+)},1}
.

Now we consider the case of the symplectic-odd orthogonal dual pairs.
For
\rho^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n^{\prime}+1}(q))
,
since
-\operatorname{id}\nolimits
is in the center of
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n^{\prime}+1}(q)
,
we know that
\rho^{\prime}(-\operatorname{id}\nolimits)=\epsilon_{\rho^{\prime}}\rho^{\prime}(\operatorname{id}\nolimits)
where
\epsilon_{\rho^{\prime}}=\pm 1
.
It is clear that if
\rho^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}(G^{\prime},s^{\prime})_{\epsilon^{\prime}}
, then
\epsilon_{\rho^{\prime}}=\epsilon^{\prime}
.
Similarly for
\rho\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q))
,
we have
\rho(-\operatorname{id}\nolimits)=\epsilon_{\rho}\rho(\operatorname{id}\nolimits)
where
\epsilon_{\rho}=\pm 1
.

Lemma 5.4
.

Let
G=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
s\in G^{*}=\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
be a semi-simple element. If
\rho\in\mathcal{E}(G,s)
, then
\rho(-\operatorname{id}\nolimits)={\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(s)\cdot\rho(\operatorname{id}\nolimits),
where
{\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}
is the spinor character of
G^{*}.

Proof.

See the proof of
[
15
, Corollary 1.22]
(see also
[
27
, Proposition 2.2.20]
).
∎

Proposition 5.5

(
[
52
]
)
.

Let
(G,G^{\prime})=(G(V),G(V^{\prime}))=(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q),\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n^{\prime}+1}(q))
,
and let
\rho\in\mathcal{E}(G,s)
and
\rho^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}(G^{\prime},s^{\prime})_{\epsilon^{\prime}}
for some semisimple elements
s\in G^{*}

and
s^{\prime}\in(G^{\prime 0})^{*}
, and some
\epsilon^{\prime}=\pm
.
Write
\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s}(\rho)=\rho^{(+)}\otimes\rho^{(-)}\otimes\rho^{(\star)}
,

\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s^{\prime}}(\rho^{\prime}|_{G^{\prime 0}})=\rho^{\prime(+)}\otimes\rho^{\prime(-)}\otimes\rho^{\prime(\star)}

where
\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s},\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s^{\prime}}
are the modified Lusztig’s Jordan decompositions.
Then
(\rho,\rho^{\prime})
occurs in
\Theta_{G,G^{\prime}}
if and only if

•

s^{(\star)}=-s^{\prime(\star)}
(up to conjugation), and
\rho^{(0)}=\rho^{\prime(0)}
;

•

\underline{G}^{(+)}\simeq G^{\prime(-)}
and
\rho^{(+)}=\rho^{\prime(-)}
;

•

(\rho^{(-)},\rho^{\prime(+)})
or
(\rho^{(-)}\cdot{\operatorname{det}},\rho^{\prime(+)})
occurs in
\Theta_{G^{(-)},\underline{G}^{\prime(+)},1}
;

•

{\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(s)=\epsilon^{\prime}
.

5.2.
Kac-Moody action on Grothendieck groups

In this section, we will obtain a complete description of the action of Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}
on the Grothendieck group of
KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits
.

5.2.1.
Ma–Qiu–Zou’s Lemma

In
[
48
, §1.8]
, Ma, Qiu and Zou introduced the concept of “theta cuspidal.” We now recall their definition. Let

(5.6)

\displaystyle\chi_{V,V^{\prime}}=\begin{cases}1&\text{ if in case $($I$)$ or $($II$)$;}\\
\zeta&\text{ if in case $($III$)$.}\end{cases}

For each
\sigma\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G_{n}),

define

c(\sigma)=\max\{k\in\mathbb{N}|\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{k}}({{}^{*}}R^{G_{n}}_{L_{n-k,k}}(\sigma),\chi_{V,V^{\prime}}\circ{\operatorname{det}}_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{k}})\neq 0\}

Clearly if
\sigma
is a cuspidal representation of
G_{n}
, then
c(\sigma)=0
. In general, we call a representation
\sigma\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G_{n})

theta cuspidal
(with respect to the dual pairs listed in §
5.1.1
)
when
c(\sigma)=0.
In particular, when
k=1
, we have the isomorphism of vector spaces

(5.7)

\displaystyle\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{1}}({{}^{*}}R^{G_{n}}_{L_{n-1,1}}(\sigma),\chi_{V,V^{\prime}})\cong E^{\epsilon}(\sigma)

which follows from the biadjointness of the functors
(E^{\pm},F^{\pm})
and isomorphisms (
2.5
) in §
2.1.2
, where
\epsilon=+
in the case
(
I
)
and
(
II
)
and
\epsilon=-
in the case
(
III
).

We will show in the following lemma that the notion of theta-cuspidal coincides with that of
F^{+}
-cuspidal or
F^{-}
-cuspidal.

Lemma 5.6
.

(a)

For cases
(
I
)
and
(
II
)
,
\sigma\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G(V))
is theta cuspidal if and only if it is
F^{+}
-cuspidal.

(b)

For case
(
III
)
,
\sigma\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G(V))
is theta cuspidal if and only if it is
F^{-}
-cuspidal.

Proof.

This follows from the definitions and the fact that
\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{n}(q)
has no irreducible quadratic unipotent cuspidal module unless
n=1
. Indeed, by isomorphisms (
5.7
), if
\sigma
is theta cuspidal, then
c(\sigma)=0
, which implies

\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{1}}({{}^{*}}R^{G_{n}}_{L_{n-1,1}}(\sigma),\chi_{V,V^{\prime}})\cong E^{\epsilon}(\sigma)=0,

hence
\sigma
is
F^{\epsilon}
-cuspidal. Conversely, if
\sigma
is
F^{\epsilon}
-cuspidal, meaning that
E^{\epsilon}(\sigma)=0
, we have

\displaystyle 0=(E^{\epsilon})^{k}(\sigma)

\displaystyle\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{1}^{\times k}}({{}^{*}}R^{G_{n}}_{L_{n-k,1^{k}}}(\sigma),\chi_{V,V^{\prime}}^{\otimes k})

\displaystyle\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{k}}({{}^{*}}R^{G_{n}}_{L_{n-k,k}}(\sigma),R_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{1}^{\times k}}^{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{k}}(\chi_{V,V^{\prime}}^{\otimes k})),

for all
k>0.
Here, the last isomorphism follows from the transitivity of Harish-Chandra restriction functors

{{}^{*}}R^{G_{n}}_{L_{n-k,1^{k}}}\cong{{}^{*}}R^{L_{n-k,k}}_{L_{n-k,1^{k}}}\circ{{}^{*}}R^{G_{n}}_{L_{n-k,k}}

and Frobenius reciprocity.
On the other hand, since the quadratic unipotent character
\chi_{V,V^{\prime}}\circ{\operatorname{det}}_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{k}}
is a constituent of
R_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{1}^{\times k}}^{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{k}}(\chi_{V,V^{\prime}}^{\otimes k})
, this forces

\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{k}}({{}^{*}}R^{G_{n}}_{L_{n-k,k}}(\sigma),\chi_{V,V^{\prime}}\circ{\operatorname{det}}_{\operatorname{GL}\nolimits_{k}})=0

for all
k>0
.
Consequently,
c(\sigma)=0,
i.e.,
\sigma
is theta cuspidal.
∎

Lemma 5.7

(
[
48
]
)
.

Let
\sigma\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G(V))
be theta cuspidal for a relative Witt towers
\mathcal{V}^{\prime}
(or
\mathcal{V}^{\prime\pm}
).

(1)

In case
(
I
)
, assume that
\sigma^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G(V^{\prime}))
(resp.

\widetilde{\sigma}^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G(\widetilde{V}^{\prime}))
) is the first occurrence of
\sigma

(resp. of
\sigma\cdot{\operatorname{det}}
) with respect to relative Witt towers
\mathcal{V}^{\prime}
, then

X^{+}(\sigma)
acts on
F^{+}(\sigma)
by the following quadratic relation

(X^{+}(\sigma)-\epsilon_{V^{\prime}}\cdot q^{\frac{\dim(V^{\prime})}{2}-\lfloor\frac{\dim(V)}{2}\rfloor})(X^{+}(\sigma)+\epsilon_{V^{\prime}}\cdot q^{\frac{\dim(\widetilde{V}^{\prime})}{2}-\lfloor\frac{\dim(V)}{2}\rfloor})=0,

where
\epsilon_{V^{\prime}}=\zeta(-1)^{\frac{\dim(V^{\prime})}{2}}.

(2)

In case
(
II
)
, assume that
\sigma^{\prime+}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G(V^{\prime+}))

(resp.
\sigma^{\prime-}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G(V^{\prime-}))
) is the first occurrence of
\sigma

with respect to relative Witt towers
\mathcal{V}^{\prime+}
(resp.
\mathcal{V}^{\prime-}
),
then
X^{+}(\sigma)
acts on
F^{+}(\sigma)
by the following quadratic relation

(X^{+}(\sigma)-q^{\frac{\dim(V^{\prime+})-\dim(V)}{2}})(X^{+}(\sigma)+q^{\frac{\dim(V^{\prime-})-\dim(V)}{2}})=0.

(3)

In case
(
III
)
,
let
\alpha=\gamma_{\psi}/\sqrt{\zeta(-1)q}
,
where
\gamma_{\psi}=\Sigma_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{q}}\psi(\frac{1}{2}x^{2})
is the Gauss sum.
Assume that
\sigma^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G(V^{\prime}))
(resp.
\widetilde{\sigma}^{\prime}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(G(\widetilde{V}^{\prime}))
) is the first occurrence of
\sigma
(resp. of
\sigma^{c}
) with respect to relative Witt towers
\mathcal{V}^{\prime}
, then
X^{-}(\sigma)
acts on
F^{-}(\sigma)
by the following quadratic relation

(X^{-}(\sigma)-\alpha\cdot q^{\lfloor\frac{\dim(V^{\prime})}{2}\rfloor-\frac{\dim(V)}{2}})(X^{-}(\sigma)+\alpha\cdot q^{\lfloor\frac{\dim(\widetilde{V}^{\prime})}{2}\rfloor-\frac{\dim(V)}{2}})=0.

Proof.

This lemma is exactly a special case of
[
48
, Lemmas 3.4, 3.5 or Proposition 3.6]
with
l=1.
Note that in
[
48
]
, they use modified Weil representation
\omega_{V,V^{\prime}}
rather than
\omega^{\psi}_{G,G^{\prime}}
defined in
[
28
]
:

(5.8)

\displaystyle\omega_{V,V^{\prime}}=\begin{cases}((\zeta\circ\det_{G(V)})^{\frac{1}{2}\dim(V^{\prime})}\otimes 1_{G(V^{\prime})})\otimes\omega^{\psi}_{G,G^{\prime}}&\text{in case $($I$)$;}\\
(1_{G(V)}\otimes(\zeta\circ\det_{G(V)})^{\frac{1}{2}\dim(V)})\otimes\omega^{\psi}_{G,G^{\prime}}&\text{in cases $($II$)$ and $($III$)$,}\end{cases}

so for case
(1)
, there is an extra sign
\epsilon_{V^{\prime}}.

Assume
G_{n}=G(V)
. For any
F^{\epsilon}
-cuspidal module
\sigma\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(KG_{n})
, the evaluation map
\phi_{F^{\epsilon}}:{\operatorname{End}}(F^{\epsilon})\to{\operatorname{End}}_{KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits}(F^{\epsilon}(\sigma))={\operatorname{End}}_{KG_{n+1}}(R_{L_{n,1}}^{G_{n+1}}(\sigma\otimes\zeta_{\epsilon}))
is surjective and
X^{\epsilon}\in{\operatorname{End}}(F^{\epsilon})
maps to
X^{\epsilon}(\sigma)\in{\operatorname{End}}_{KG_{n+1}}(R_{L_{n,1}}^{G_{n+1}}(\sigma\otimes\zeta_{\epsilon}))
, where
\zeta_{\epsilon}=1
if
\epsilon=+
and
\zeta_{\epsilon}=\zeta
if
\epsilon=-
.
Then
X^{\epsilon}(\sigma)
is identified with a scalar multiple of “unnormalized Hecke operator”
T_{l}
defined in
[
48
, §3.2]
for the case
l=1
. In fact,

(5.9)

\displaystyle X^{\epsilon}(\sigma)=\begin{cases}q^{-\lfloor\frac{1}{2}\dim(V)\rfloor}T_{l}&\text{in cases $($I$)$ and $($II$)$ with $\epsilon=+$; }\\
\sqrt{\zeta(-1)}\,q^{-\frac{\dim(V)+1}{2}}T_{l}&\text{in case $($III$)$ with $\epsilon=-$.}\end{cases}

Then the lemma follows from
[
48
, Proposition 3.6]
immediately.
∎

Remark 5.8
.

Note that the Gauss sum
\gamma_{\psi}=\pm\sqrt{\zeta(-1)q}
, and thus

\alpha\in\{\pm 1\}
.
Consequently, Lemma
5.7
and Proposition
4.11
together imply that the sets
I_{+}
and
I_{-}
are both equal to
q^{\mathbb{Z}}\sqcup-q^{\mathbb{Z}}
, which aligns with the result stated in Proposition
4.9
.

5.2.2.
Unipotent case

Before dealing with the general case, we first deal with the unipotent case.

Theorem 5.9
.

(a)

If
G_{\bullet}=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2\bullet}(q),
then

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits}_{t})=(u-(-q)^{t})(u-(-q)^{-1-t}).

(b)

Let
G_{\bullet}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2\bullet}(q)
and
t\in\mathbb{N}
,
then

\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{t}=\pi_{t}^{\beta}\quad\text{and}\,\,\quad\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{-t}=\pi_{t}^{\alpha}.

Proof.

(a)

We consider the symplectic-even orthogonal dual pair. Write
\epsilon_{k}=(-1)^{k}
. Let
\sigma=\rho^{\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits}_{t}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2(t^{2}+t)}(q))
be the unique irreducible unipotent cuspidal module.
By Theorem
5.1
, we know that
\sigma
first occurs in the correspondences
for both dual pairs

(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2(t^{2}+t)}(q),\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t}}_{2t^{2}}(q))\quad\text{and}\,\,\quad(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2(t^{2}+t)}(q),\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t+1}}_{2(t+1)^{2}}(q)).

By Lemma
5.7
(2)
, we know that
X^{+}(\sigma)
acts on
F^{+}(\sigma)
satisfying

(X^{+}(\sigma)-(-q)^{t})(X^{+}(\sigma)-(-q)^{-1-t})=0.

Then by Lemma
4.6
,

(a)
follows.

(b)
We consider even orthogonal-symplectic dual pair. Let

\sigma=\pi^{\beta}_{t}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t}}_{2t^{2}}(q)),

then
\sigma\cdot{\operatorname{det}}=\pi^{\alpha}_{t}
.
We know that
\sigma=\pi^{\beta}_{t}
first occurs in the correspondence
for dual pair
(\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t}}_{2t^{2}}(q),\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2t(t-1)}(q))

and
\sigma\cdot{\operatorname{det}}=\pi^{\alpha}_{t}
first occurs in the correspondence
for dual pair
(\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t}}_{2t^{2}}(q),\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2t(t+1)}(q)).

Note that
\frac{\dim(V^{\prime})}{2}
is an even number, so
\epsilon_{V^{\prime}}=\zeta(-1)^{\frac{\dim(V^{\prime})}{2}}=1.

By Lemma
5.7

(1)
, we know that
X^{+}(\sigma)
acts on
F^{+}(\sigma)
satisfying

(X^{+}(\sigma)-q^{t})(X^{+}(\sigma)+q^{-t})=0.

Then by Lemma
4.6
,
we know
\pi_{t}^{\beta}=\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{t}
. A similar argument implies
\pi_{t}^{\alpha}=\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{-t}
.
∎

Remark 5.10
.

Note that, for the case of unipotent cuspidal modules of
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
,
this result coincides with
[
19
, Theorem 6.5]
.
The above theorem gives a new proof of characteristic 0. Using unitary-unitary theta correspondence
[
48
, Proposition 3.6]
, a similar argument also applies to the unitary groups
\operatorname{GU}\nolimits_{n}(q)
case, which gives a new proof of
[
20
, Theorem 4.12]
.

Remark 5.11
.

Conversely, if we know the colored weight function
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)
for unipotent cuspidal modules
\rho
, then by Lemma
5.7
, we can determine the two first occurrences of
\rho
via
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)
. In particular, Dudas, Varagnolo and Vasserot
[
19
, Theorem 6.5]
proved that for symplectic groups
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q),
we have
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho^{\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits}_{t})=(u-(-q)^{t})(u-(-q)^{-1-t})
, then by Lemma
5.7
, one can show that
\rho^{\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits}_{t}
first occurs in the theta correspondence for the dual pairs
(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2t(t+1)}(q),\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t+1}}_{2(t+1)^{2}}(q))
and
(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2t(t+1)}(q),\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t}}_{2t^{2}}(q)),
which gives a new proof of Theorem
5.1
. Moverover, by
[
48
, Theorem 1.3]
, one can recover the symplectic-even orthogonal theta correspondence for unipotent characters.

5.2.3.
General case

Now we compute
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(-)
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(-)
for all irreducible modules which are both

F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal.

We first introduce a lemma to compute the spinor character for semisimple elements of orthogonal groups. Let
G=G(V)
be an orthogonal group and
s\in G
be a semisimple element. Let
s=\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}}s_{\Gamma}
be a primary decomposition of
s
. Recall that we denote by
\eta_{\Gamma}=\eta_{\Gamma}(s)
the type of
V_{\Gamma}=V_{\Gamma}(s)
,
\delta_{\Gamma}
the reduced degree of
\Gamma
, and
m_{\Gamma}=m_{\Gamma}(s)
the multiplicity of
(\Gamma)
in
s_{\Gamma}
. Suppose that
\alpha
is a root of
\Gamma
. Let
\sigma:\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}\to\{\pm 1\}
be defined by

\displaystyle\sigma(\Gamma)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $\alpha\in(\mathbb{F}^{\times}_{q^{\delta_{\Gamma}}})^{2}$ and $\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}$};\\
1&\text{if $\alpha^{(q^{\delta_{\Gamma}}+1)/2}=1$ and $\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{2}$};\\
-1&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Lemma 5.12
.

Let
G=G(V)
be an orthogonal group. If
s\in G^{0},
we have

(5.10)

\displaystyle{\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(s)=\begin{cases}\zeta(-1)^{\frac{\dim(V_{x+1})}{2}}\cdot\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2},\sigma(\Gamma)\neq 1}(-1)^{m_{\Gamma}(s)}&\text{if $\eta_{x+1}(s)=1$};\\
-\zeta(-1)^{\frac{\dim(V_{x+1})}{2}}\cdot\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2},\sigma(\Gamma)\neq 1}(-1)^{m_{\Gamma}(s)}&\text{if $\eta_{x+1}(s)=-1$}.\end{cases}

Proof.

This is
[
12
, Proposition 16.30]
.
∎

Now we define some constants that occur in colored weight functions.
Let
\rho=\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)}
be both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal, where
\lambda_{\star}=\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}\lambda_{\Gamma}.

For
G=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
and
\rho=\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}},
we define

(5.11)

\displaystyle\eta(\rho)=\eta_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}}=(-1)^{t_{+}+t_{-}}\cdot\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}}(-1)^{|\lambda_{\Gamma}|}.

For
G=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
and
\rho=\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon}
, we define

(5.12)

\displaystyle\eta^{+}(\rho)=\eta^{+}_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon}=\epsilon\cdot(-1)^{t_{+}}\cdot\prod_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2},\sigma(\Gamma)\neq 1}(-1)^{|\lambda_{\Gamma}|},

and

(5.13)

\displaystyle\eta^{-}(\rho)=\eta^{-}_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon}=\epsilon\cdot(-1)^{t_{-}}\cdot\prod_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2},\sigma(\Gamma)\neq 1}(-1)^{|\lambda_{\Gamma}|}.

Note that
\eta(\rho),\eta^{\delta}(\rho)\in\{\pm 1\}
for
\delta\in\{\pm\}.
Then we have the following theorem.

Theorem 5.13
.

Let
\rho=\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},(\epsilon)}
be both
F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal.

(a)

If
G_{\bullet}=\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2\bullet}(q),
then

(a1)

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}})=(u-\eta_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}}\cdot q^{t_{+}})(u+\eta_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}}\cdot q^{-1-t_{+}}),

(a2)

\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}})=(v-q^{t_{-}})(v+q^{-t_{-}}).

(b)

If
G_{\bullet}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2\bullet}(q)
, then

(b1)

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}})=(u-q^{t_{+}})(u+q^{-t_{+}}),

(b2)

\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}})=(v-q^{t_{-}})(v+q^{-t_{-}}).

(c)

If
G_{\bullet}=\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2\bullet+1}(q)
, then

(c1)

\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon})=(u-\eta^{+}_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon}\cdot q^{t_{+}})(u+\eta^{+}_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon}\cdot q^{-1-t_{+}}),

(c2)

\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon})=(v-\eta^{-}_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon}\cdot q^{t_{-}})(v+\eta^{-}_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon}\cdot q^{-1-t_{-}}).

Proof.

We first prove
(a1)

by using the theta correspondence of dual pair
(G,G^{\prime})=(\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q),\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}_{2n^{\prime}}(q)).

Let
(\rho,\rho^{\prime+})
(resp.
(\rho,\rho^{\prime-})
) be the first occurrence of dual pair
(G,G^{\prime})=(G(V),G(V^{\prime+}))
(resp.
(G(V),G(V^{\prime-}))
) with respect to
\mathcal{V}^{\prime+}
(resp.
\mathcal{V}^{\prime-}
). Assume that
\rho\in\mathcal{E}(G,s)
and
\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s}(\rho)=\rho^{(+)}\otimes\rho^{(-)}\otimes\rho^{(\star)}.

Then
s\in(G^{*})^{0}=G_{0}(V^{*})
determines a decomposition

V^{*}=V^{*}_{x-1}\oplus V^{*}_{x+1}\oplus\bigoplus_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}V^{*}_{\Gamma}

such that

(\underline{G}^{(+)})^{*}=G_{0}(V^{*}_{x-1}),\quad G^{(-)}=G(V^{*}_{x+1}),\quad G^{(\star)}=\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}C_{G(V^{*}_{\Gamma})}(s_{\Gamma}),

where
V^{*}_{x-1}
and
V^{*}_{x+1}
are both orthogonal spaces.

Let
V_{x-1}
be a symplectic space such that
G(V_{x-1})=\underline{G}^{(+)}=G_{0}(V^{*}_{x-1})^{*}.

Then we have
\dim(V_{x-1})=\dim(V^{*}_{x-1})-1.

Similarly, for
\epsilon\in\{\pm\}
, assume that
\rho^{\prime\epsilon}\in\mathcal{E}(G^{\prime},s^{\prime})
and
\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s^{\prime}}(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})=(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(+)}\otimes(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(-)}\otimes(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(\star)}.
Then
s^{\prime}\in G^{\prime*}=G((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*})
determines the decomposition

(V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}=(V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1}\oplus(V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x+1}\oplus\bigoplus_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}(V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{\Gamma}

such that

\underline{G}^{\prime(+)}=G((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1}),\quad G^{\prime(-)}=G((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x+1}),\quad G^{\prime(\star)}=\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}C_{G((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{\Gamma})}(s^{\prime}_{\Gamma}),

where
(V^{\prime\epsilon})_{x-1}^{*}
and
(V^{\prime\epsilon})_{x+1}^{*}
are both orthogonal spaces.

In fact, by
[
53
, Lemma 3.15]
and Theorem
4.3
,
we have
\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s}(\rho)=\rho^{\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits}_{t_{+}}\otimes\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{\pm t_{-}}\otimes\rho_{\lambda_{\star}}
, i.e.,
\rho^{(+)}=\rho^{\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits}_{t_{+}}
and
\rho^{(-)}=\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{t_{-}}
or
\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{-t_{-}}
and
\rho^{(\star)}=\rho_{\lambda_{\star}}.

By the commutativity of theta correspondence and modified Lusztig’s Jordan decomposition (see Proposition
5.3
), we must have

•

V^{*}_{\Gamma}\cong(V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{\Gamma}
,
s_{\Gamma}=s^{\prime}_{\Gamma}
for any
\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}
and
\rho^{(\star)}=(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(\star)}
;

•

V^{*}_{x+1}\cong(V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x+1}
and
\rho^{(-)}=(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(-)}
or
\rho^{(-)}=(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(-)}\cdot{\operatorname{det}}
;

•

\rho^{(+)}\otimes(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(+)}
or
\rho^{(+)}\otimes((\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(+)}\cdot{\operatorname{det}})
first occurs in
\omega_{\underline{G}^{(+)},\underline{G}^{\prime(+)},1}
for the symplectic-even orthogonal theta dual pair
(V_{x-1},(V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1})
.

In other words, we must have

•

(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(\star)}=\rho_{\lambda_{\star}}
,

•

(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(-)}=\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{\pm t_{-}}
,

•

if
\eta((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1})=\epsilon_{t_{+}}
, then
(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(+)}=\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{\pm t_{+}}
and
(\rho^{\prime-\epsilon})^{(+)}=\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{\pm(t_{+}-1)}
and if
\eta((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1})=\epsilon_{t_{+}-1}
, then

(\rho^{\prime\epsilon})^{(+)}=\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{\pm(t_{+}-1)}
and
(\rho^{\prime-\epsilon})^{(+)}=\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{\pm t_{+}}
,

where
\epsilon_{k}=(-1)^{k}
for
k=t_{+}
and
t_{+}-1
.

Note that
\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{\pm t_{-}}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t_{-}}}_{2(t_{-})^{2}}),

\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{\pm t_{+}}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t_{+}}}_{2(t_{+})^{2}})
and
\rho^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{\mathrm{even}}}_{\pm(t_{+}-1)}\in{\operatorname{Irr}\nolimits}(\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\epsilon_{t_{+}-1}}_{2(t_{+}-1)^{2}}).

Morover, we have
\epsilon=\eta(V^{\prime\epsilon})=\eta((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*})
, which is equal to

\eta((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1})\eta((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x+1})\eta(\bigoplus_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}(V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{\Gamma}).

Since
\eta((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1})=\epsilon_{t_{+}}
or
\epsilon_{t_{+}-1}
,
\eta((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x+1})=\epsilon_{t_{-}}=(-1)^{t_{-}}
and

\eta(\bigoplus_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}(V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{\Gamma})=\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}}(-1)^{m_{\Gamma}(s^{\prime})}=\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}}(-1)^{m_{\Gamma}(s)}=\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}}(-1)^{|\lambda_{\Gamma}|},

we know that if
\eta((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1})=\epsilon_{t_{+}}
, then
\epsilon=\eta_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star}},
and if
\eta((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1})=\epsilon_{t_{+}-1}
, then
\epsilon=\eta_{t_{+}-1,t_{-},\lambda_{\star}}.

On the other hand, we know that
\dim(V^{*}_{x+1})=\dim((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x+1})
and
\dim(\bigoplus\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}V^{*}_{\Gamma})=\dim(\bigoplus\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}(V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{\Gamma})
, so

\displaystyle\dim(V)-\dim(V^{\prime\epsilon})

\displaystyle=\dim(V^{*})-1-\dim((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*})

\displaystyle=\big(\dim(V^{*}_{x-1})+\dim(V^{*}_{x+1})+\sum\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}\dim(V^{*}_{\Gamma})\big)-1

\displaystyle-\big(\dim((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1})+\dim((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x+1})+\sum\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}\dim((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{\Gamma})\big)

\displaystyle=\dim(V^{*}_{x-1})-\dim((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1})-1

\displaystyle=\dim(V_{x-1})-\dim((V^{\prime\epsilon})^{*}_{x-1}).

Then
(a1)
follows from Lemma

(2)
.

Note that

and

hold true by the definitions.

(c)
By extra symmetries (see Proposition
4.11
), we have

\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon})=\mathbb{O}^{+}(v)({\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}\cdot\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon})=\mathbb{O}^{+}(v)(\rho_{t_{-},t_{+},(-\lambda)_{\star},{\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(-\operatorname{id}\nolimits)\cdot\epsilon}),

where
(-\lambda)_{\star}
is defined by
(-\lambda)_{\star}=\prod\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}\lambda_{-\Gamma}
and
-\Gamma
is defined by
(-\Gamma)(x)=(-1)^{\deg(\Gamma)}\cdot\Gamma(-x)
.
By definition,

\eta^{+}_{t_{-},t_{+},(-\lambda)_{\star},{\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(-\operatorname{id}\nolimits)\cdot\epsilon}={\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(-\operatorname{id}\nolimits)\cdot\epsilon\cdot(-1)^{t_{-}}\cdot\prod_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2},\sigma(-\Gamma)\neq 1}(-1)^{|\lambda_{\Gamma}|}.

Assume that
\rho\in\mathcal{E}(G,s)
and
\underline{\mathcal{J}}_{s}(\rho|_{G^{0}})=\rho^{(+)}\otimes\rho^{(-)}\otimes\rho^{(\star)}.
Then
s\in(G^{*})^{0}=G(V^{*})
determines a decomposition

(5.14)

\displaystyle V^{*}=V^{*}_{x-1}\oplus V^{*}_{x+1}\oplus\bigoplus_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}V^{*}_{\Gamma}.

We have that
\dim(V^{*})=\dim(V^{*}_{x-1})+\dim(V^{*}_{x+1})+\sum\limits_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}\dim(V^{*}_{x+1})
,
\dim(V^{*}_{x-1})=2t_{+}(t_{+}+1)
,
\dim(V^{*}_{x+1})=2t_{-}(t_{-}+1)
and
\dim(V^{*}_{\Gamma})=2\delta_{\Gamma}m_{\Gamma}(s)=2\delta_{\Gamma}|\lambda_{\Gamma}|,

so

{\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(-\operatorname{id}\nolimits)=\zeta(-1)^{\frac{\dim{V}-1}{2}}=\zeta(-1)^{\frac{\dim{V^{*}}}{2}}=\prod_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}\zeta(-1)^{\delta_{\Gamma}|\lambda_{\Gamma}|}.

On the other hand, under the decomposition (
5.14
),
s=s^{(+)}\times s^{(-)}\times s^{(\star)}
. We consider
s^{(\star)}\in\operatorname{O}\nolimits^{\pm}((V^{*})^{(\star)})
, where
(V^{*})^{(\star)}=\bigoplus_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}V^{*}_{\Gamma}
, then we have
{\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(s^{(\star)})={\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(-s^{(\star)}){\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(-\operatorname{id}\nolimits_{(V^{*})^{(\star)}})
. So we have

\prod_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2},\sigma(-\Gamma)\neq 1}(-1)^{|\lambda_{\Gamma}|}=\prod_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2},\sigma(\Gamma)\neq 1}(-1)^{|\lambda_{\Gamma}|}\cdot\prod_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{F}_{1}\cup\mathcal{F}_{2}}\zeta(-1)^{\delta_{\Gamma}|\lambda_{\Gamma}|},

i.e.,
\eta^{-}_{t_{+},t_{-},\lambda_{\star},\epsilon}=\eta^{+}_{t_{-},t_{+},(-\lambda)_{\star},{\operatorname{sp}\nolimits}(-\operatorname{id}\nolimits)\cdot\epsilon}.

Hence if we can prove
(c1)
, then
(c2)

follows by the definition.

Remark 5.14
.

Specifically, when considering quadratic unipotent modules (i.e.,
\lambda_{\star}=\emptyset
), the corresponding signs appear notably simpler. For the symplectic group
\operatorname{Sp}\nolimits_{2n}(q)
, we have
\eta(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-}})=(-1)^{t_{+}+t_{-}}.

For the odd orthogonal group
\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
, we have
\eta^{+}(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\epsilon})=\epsilon\cdot(-1)^{t_{+}}
and
\eta^{-}(\rho_{t_{+},t_{-},\epsilon})=\epsilon\cdot(-1)^{t_{-}}
.
Via the restriction functor
\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^{\operatorname{O}\nolimits_{n+1}}_{\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}}
, one can show that this gives a new proof of
[
39
, Theorem 5.17]
for quadratic unipotent modules of
\operatorname{SO}\nolimits_{2n+1}(q)
.

Remark 5.15
.

Note that the theta correspondence depends on the choices of the non-trivial character
\psi:(\mathbb{F}_{q},+)\to\mathbb{C}^{\times}.
However, the colored weight functions are independent of choices of
\psi
and the theta correspondence.

5.2.4.
Kac-Moody action on Grothendieck groups

The
ambiguity in the determination of colored weight functions for all irreducible modules that are simultaneously

F^{+}
-cuspidal and
F^{-}
-cuspidal, as originally stated in Theorem
4.21
, has now been successfully resolved.
As a consequence, we have the following theorem.

Theorem 5.16
.

The pairs
(s^{+}_{1},s^{+}_{2})
and
(s^{-}_{1},s^{-}_{2})
in Theorem
4.21
are given in Table
4
by
\mathbb{O}^{+}(u)(\rho)=(u-q^{s^{+}_{1}})(u+q^{s^{+}_{2}})
and
\mathbb{O}^{-}(v)(\rho)=(v-q^{s^{-}_{1}})(v+q^{s^{-}_{2}})
.

Hence colored weight functions of all irreducible modules are determined explicitly and the action of Kac-Moody algebra
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{+}}\oplus\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{l}^{\prime}_{I_{-}}

on the Grothendieck group
[KG_{\bullet}\operatorname{-mod}\nolimits]
is completely determined.

Question: Under the parametrization via our complete invariants, how can the finite theta correspondence be explicitly described? For unipotent modules within the symplectic-even orthogonal dual pair, this is addressed by Theorem
5.9
. Pan
[
53
]
demonstrated that the modified Lusztig’s Jordan decomposition for a classical group can be rendered unique provided it is required to be compatible with parabolic induction and a specific finite theta correspondence with a fixed non-trivial character
\psi.
Wang
[
60
]
showed that, when
q
is sufficiently large, there exists a unique choice of the modified Lusztig correspondence that is compatible with parabolic induction and the theta correspondence for all dual pairs. This question is essentially equivalent to exploring the relationship between colored weight functions and modified Lusztig’s Jordan decompositions defined by Pan
[
53
, §8,§9]
and Wang
[
60
, Theorem 6.1]
.
